86586.q: What happens when you click on a link?
86586.e: A link takes you to another page or another place. That is why the browser jumps there.
86586.m: A link takes you to another page.

86587.q: What shape does the mouse pointer often take when it is over a link?
86587.e: Over a link, the arrow often turns into a small hand with a pointing finger. That way you know you can click there.
86587.m: The small hand shows you a link.

86588.q: What do text links on web pages often look like?
86588.e: Many websites show links in blue with a line underneath. But some pages design links differently.
86588.m: Blue, underlined words are often links.

86589.q: Can a picture be a link too?
86589.e: Pictures and buttons can be links too. If you click on them, another page opens.

86590.q: What should you do with a link in a message from a stranger?
86590.e: Links from strangers can lead to dangerous pages. Better to ask an adult.
86590.m: I do not click on links from strangers.

86591.q: Why is the web called a “web”?
a: Because it is made of string
86591.e: Countless links connect the web pages with each other. That makes a web, like a spider's web.
86591.m: Links connect web pages into a web.

86592.q: What do you usually tap a link with on a tablet?
86592.e: On a tablet or phone you tap the link with your finger. On a computer you usually use the mouse.
86592.m: On a tablet you tap links with your finger.

86593.q: Which three letters do many web addresses begin with?
86593.e: Many addresses begin with www, for example www.sbb.ch. But some addresses also work without www.
86593.m: Many web addresses begin with www.

86594.q: Which character separates the parts of a web address like www.sbb.ch?
86594.e: In a web address there are dots between the parts. You say, for example, “www dot sbb dot ch”.
86594.m: In web addresses there are dots between the parts.

86595.q: What usually happens if you make a typing mistake in a web address?
a: You end up on the wrong page.
86595.e: The computer looks for exactly the address you type. If one letter is wrong, you get an error message or a different page.
86595.m: You must type web addresses exactly right.

86596.q: Can a web address contain a space?
86596.e: Web addresses have no spaces. Instead of a space there is sometimes a hyphen.
86596.m: Web addresses are written without spaces.

86597.q: How many times does the same web address exist on the whole internet?
86597.e: Every web address is unique, like a home address. That way the computer always finds the right page.
86597.m: Each web address exists only once.

86598.q: Which ending do many web addresses from Switzerland have?
86598.e: The ending .ch comes from the Latin name Confoederatio Helvetica. The federal government uses it too, for example in admin.ch.
86598.m: Swiss web addresses often end in .ch.

86599.q: What do web addresses with a protected connection begin with?
86599.e: The s at the end of https stands for “secure”. The data is then sent encrypted.
86599.m: With https the connection is protected.

86600.q: What did the ending .com in a web address originally stand for?
86600.e: .com comes from the word “commercial” and was meant for companies. Today, though, many different websites use it.
86600.m: The ending .com was originally meant for companies.

86601.q: What is it called when you copy a file from the internet onto your device?
86601.e: Getting a file from the internet is a download. Upload is the opposite, sending a file to the internet.
86601.m: Getting a file from the internet is called downloading.

86602.q: What happens when you download a file?
a: It is saved on your device.
86602.e: When downloading, your device fetches a file from the internet. After that it is saved on your device.
86602.m: What you download is then on your device.

86603.q: What is the opposite of downloading?
86603.e: When uploading, you send a file from your device to the internet. When downloading, you fetch it from the internet.
86603.m: Uploading is the opposite of downloading.

86604.q: Which symbol often stands for downloading?
86604.e: An arrow pointing down shows that something is coming from the internet onto your device. An arrow pointing up often stands for uploading.
86604.m: An arrow pointing down means downloading.

86605.q: What takes the longest to download?
86605.e: A film is a very big file. The bigger a file is, the longer it takes to download.
86605.m: Big files take longer to download.

86606.q: Who do you ask before you download something?
a: A child you do not know in a chat
86606.e: Some files can be dangerous or cost money. That is why children ask an adult first.
86606.m: Before downloading, you ask an adult.

86607.q: In which folder do downloaded files often end up on a computer?
86607.e: Most computers save downloaded files in the “Downloads” folder. That is where you find them again.
86607.m: You often find downloaded files in the “Downloads” folder.

86608.q: What can a downloaded file from an unknown site contain?
86608.e: A computer virus is a harmful program. It can hide in files that you download.
86608.m: Files from unknown sites can contain viruses.

86609.q: Which word does the word “app” come from?
86609.e: App is short for “application”. That means a program you use.

86610.q: Where do you download new apps on a phone?
86610.e: An app store is a shop for apps on a phone or tablet. Some apps are free, others cost money.
86610.m: You get apps from an app store.

86611.q: What are the small pictures on the screen that you use to open an app called?
86611.e: Every app has a small picture called an icon. If you tap it, the app starts.
86611.m: You open an app by tapping its icon.

86612.q: What does an update do to an app?
86612.e: With an update the app is improved. Bugs are fixed and sometimes new things are added.
86612.m: An update makes an app better.

86613.q: Which app on a phone shows you what time it is?
86613.e: The clock app shows the time. Often it also has an alarm and a stopwatch.
86613.m: The clock app shows you the time.

86614.q: What can you do with an app that you no longer need?
86614.e: You can remove unnecessary apps from your device. That gives you more storage space again.
86614.m: You can delete apps you do not need.

86615.q: What do many apps need so that everything works?
86615.e: Many apps fetch data from the internet, for example weather or news. Without a connection that does not work.

86616.q: What does a weather app show?
a: What the weather will be like
86616.e: A weather app fetches weather data from the internet. It shows, for example, whether it is raining or the sun is shining.
86616.m: A weather app shows the weather.

86617.e: A server is a computer that delivers things to other computers, for example web pages or videos. The word comes from “to serve”.
86617.m: A server delivers data to other computers.

86618.q: When do most servers on the internet work?
86618.e: People all over the world need the internet at all times. That is why servers run without a break.

86619.q: What does a server deliver when you watch a video on the internet?
86619.e: The video is stored on a server. The server sends it to your device bit by bit.
86619.m: Videos on the internet come from servers.

86620.q: What does a server need to work?
86620.e: A server is a computer and needs electricity. That is why lots of servers use a lot of energy.

86621.q: Why are rooms with lots of servers cooled?
a: Because the servers want to feel cold
Because otherwise it is too loud
86621.e: Servers work hard and get hot doing it. They are cooled so that they do not break.
86621.m: Servers are cooled because they get warm.

86622.q: How many people can fetch data from a server at the same time?
86622.e: A server can answer lots of requests at the same time. That is why lots of people can look at the same page.
86622.m: A server serves lots of people at the same time.

86623.q: Where are your messages often stored before they reach your friend?
86623.e: When you send a message, it goes to a server first. From there it is sent on to your friend.

86624.q: What happens when a website's server breaks down?
86624.e: The website is on the server. If the server is broken or switched off, nobody can open the page.
86624.m: Without its server, a website cannot be reached.

86625.q: What does the router do at home?
a: It connects the devices to the internet.
86625.e: The router is the little box that connects your home to the internet. All devices send their data through it.
86625.m: The router brings the internet into your home.

86626.q: What does the router at home share with phones and tablets without a cable?
86626.e: Most routers send out Wi-Fi. Devices connect to it without a cable.
86626.m: The router sends out the Wi-Fi.

86627.q: What do the little lights on the router show?
86627.e: The lights show whether the router has power and is connected to the internet. If a light is red, there is often a problem.
86627.m: The lights on the router show whether everything is working.

86628.q: What often helps when the internet at home is not working?
86628.e: You switch the router off and on again after a short time. After that it often connects properly again.

86629.q: What can a router be compared to?
86629.e: The router sends data to the right address, like a postman delivers letters. That way every message reaches the right device.
86629.m: A router delivers data like a postman delivers letters.

86630.q: What do you need to connect to the router's Wi-Fi?
86630.e: Wi-Fi is usually protected with a password. Only people who know it can connect.
86630.m: Wi-Fi is protected with a password.

86631.q: What can you use to connect a computer to the router without Wi-Fi?
86631.e: You plug a network cable into the computer and the router. The connection through the cable is often faster and more stable than Wi-Fi.
86631.m: With a network cable you connect devices without Wi-Fi.

86632.q: Where in the flat is the Wi-Fi usually strongest?
a: Very far away from the router
86632.e: The signal comes from the router. The further away you are, the weaker it gets.
86632.m: The Wi-Fi is strongest close to the router.

86633.q: How many devices can be connected to a router at the same time?
86633.e: Phone, tablet, computer and television can all be connected to the router at the same time. The router shares the connection.
86633.m: A router connects several devices at the same time.

86634.e: Submarine cables lie on the floor of the sea. They connect countries and continents.
86634.m: Submarine cables lie on the seabed.

86635.e: Submarine cables run, for example, from Europe to America. That way the internet is connected all over the world.

86636.q: How does most internet data get from Europe to America?
86636.e: Almost all the data between continents travels through cables in the sea. Satellites carry only a small part.
86636.m: Most data between continents travels through submarine cables.

86637.q: What travels through the glass fibres in modern submarine cables?
86637.e: In the thin glass fibres, the data travels as light signals. Light is very fast.
86637.m: In fibre-optic cables data travels as light.

86638.q: What are submarine cables laid with?
86638.e: Cable layers are big ships with huge reels of cable. They slowly let the cable sink to the seabed.
86638.m: Special ships lay the submarine cables.

86639.q: What can damage a submarine cable?
86639.e: Anchors and fishing nets can damage submarine cables. Then a ship has to repair the cable.
86639.m: Anchors and fishing nets can damage submarine cables.

86640.q: How is Switzerland connected to the submarine cables?
86640.e: Switzerland is not by the sea. That is why cables run over land to the coasts, where the submarine cables begin.
86640.m: Switzerland is connected to the submarine cables by land cables.

86641.q: What was the first thing sent through a cable across the Atlantic more than 150 years ago?
86641.e: In 1858 the first cable was laid across the Atlantic. It carried telegrams, which are short messages. There was no internet back then.
86641.m: The first Atlantic cable carried telegrams.

86642.e: Online means that a device is connected to the internet. Then you can open web pages.
86642.m: When you are online, you are connected to the internet.

86643.e: Offline means that a device has no connection to the internet at the moment. The device can still be switched on.
86643.m: When you are offline, you are not connected to the internet.

86644.q: What happens to a phone when you switch on aeroplane mode?
86644.e: In aeroplane mode the phone switches off its wireless connections. That is why it is offline, but it stays switched on.
86644.m: In aeroplane mode the phone is offline.

86645.q: What can you do offline too?
86645.e: Photos on your device are already saved. You do not need the internet for that.

a: A game played over the internet
86646.e: In an online game you are connected to the internet. Often you play with other people.
86646.m: Online games are played over the internet.

86647.q: What is a good idea when you have been online for a long time?
86647.e: Breaks are good for your eyes and your body. Playing, being outside or reading work offline too.
86647.m: Breaks from the screen do you good.

86648.q: What often appears on the screen when a device has no internet connection?
86648.e: If the device is offline, the browser or app shows a message. Often it says “No connection”.
86648.m: The message “No connection” shows that you are offline.

86649.q: What are maps called that you save before a trip so they work without the internet?
86649.e: Offline maps are loaded onto the device beforehand. Then you do not need the internet on the way.
86649.m: Offline maps work without the internet.

86650.q: In a chat app, what does a green dot next to a name often show?
86650.e: Many apps use a green dot to show that someone is online right now. If the dot is missing, the person is usually offline.
86650.m: A green dot often shows that someone is online.

86651.q: Along with the web, what did Tim Berners-Lee invent for looking at web pages?
86651.e: In 1990 at CERN, Tim Berners-Lee programmed the first web browser himself. He called it WorldWideWeb.
86651.m: Tim Berners-Lee also wrote the first web browser.

86652.q: In which country is the research centre CERN, where Tim Berners-Lee invented the web?
86652.e: Tim Berners-Lee worked at CERN near Geneva. That is where the World Wide Web was born.
86652.m: The web was invented at CERN near Geneva.

86653.q: Which country does Tim Berners-Lee come from?
86653.e: Tim Berners-Lee was born in London in 1955. He is English.

86654.q: What does the abbreviation www stand for?
86654.e: www means World Wide Web, a network that spans the world. Tim Berners-Lee invented it.

86655.q: How much money did Tim Berners-Lee ask for so that everyone could use the web?
86655.e: He wanted the web to belong to everyone. That is why the web is free for everyone to use.
86655.m: The web is a gift to everyone.

86656.q: In which year did the first website go online?
86656.e: The first website went online at CERN in 1991. It explained what the web is.
86656.m: The first website went online in 1991.

86657.q: Which title of honour did Tim Berners-Lee receive from the British Queen?
86657.e: The Queen knighted him in 2004. Since then he has been called Sir Tim Berners-Lee.
86657.m: Tim Berners-Lee has the title Sir.

86658.q: What did a note on the world's first web server say?
86658.e: Tim Berners-Lee's computer had a note stuck on it saying: this machine is a server, do not power it down! Otherwise the whole web would no longer have been reachable.
86658.m: The first web server was not allowed to be switched off.

86659.q: What is special about a search engine for children?
a: It is only open at night.
86659.e: Adults check the pages beforehand. That way the children's search engine only shows pages that are suitable for children.
86659.m: Children's search engines show checked pages.

86660.q: What is the list that a search engine shows after searching called?
86660.e: After searching, the search engine shows a list of matching pages. Each page in this list is a result.
86660.m: The search engine shows you a list of results.

86661.q: Which of these is a search engine for children?
86661.e: fragFINN is a search engine for children. It only finds checked pages.
86661.m: fragFINN is a search engine for children.

86662.q: What do you do to open a page you have found in the search engine?
86662.e: Every search result is a link. When you click or tap on it, the page opens.
86662.m: You open a search result with a click.

86663.q: What do you type into a children's search engine?
86663.e: You type in a word, for example “hedgehog”. Then the search engine shows matching pages.
86663.m: You type a search word into a search engine.

86664.q: What do you do if you find something strange in the children's search engine?
86664.e: Even a children's search engine is not perfect. Tell an adult if something seems strange to you.
86664.m: With strange pages, I fetch an adult.

86665.q: Compared with a normal search engine, how many results does a children's search engine usually show?
86665.e: Children's search engines only search selected pages. That is why there are fewer, but more suitable, results.
86665.m: Children's search engines show fewer but suitable results.

86666.q: Who checks the pages for a children's search engine?
86666.e: Experts look at the pages before they go on the list. That keeps unsuitable pages out.
86666.m: Experts check the pages for children's search engines.

86667.q: Can you eat a fly agaric?
86667.e: The fly agaric is a poisonous mushroom. You must never eat it.
86667.m: Leave the pretty fly agaric where it is in the forest.

86668.q: Under which trees does the fly agaric often grow?
86668.e: The fly agaric lives together with birches and spruces. That is why you often find it under these trees.
86668.m: The fly agaric likes to grow near birches and spruces.

86669.q: What colour are the gills of the fly agaric?
86669.e: Under the red cap, the gills of the fly agaric are white. They are packed closely together.
86669.m: Under the red cap of the fly agaric everything is white.

86670.q: Where does the fly agaric get its name from?
a: People used to catch flies with it
It can fly through the air
86670.e: In the past, people put pieces of the mushroom in milk. Flies that drank it were stunned or died.
86670.m: People used the fly agaric to fight flies.

86671.q: What colour is the stem of the fly agaric?
86671.e: The stem of the fly agaric is white and has a thick bulb at the bottom. Only the cap is red.
86671.m: The fly agaric has a white stem.

86672.q: What can happen to the white spots of a fly agaric after heavy rain?
86672.e: The white flakes only sit loosely on the cap. Heavy rain can wash them off, and then the cap is almost all red.
86672.m: Rain can wash the white spots off a fly agaric.

86673.q: What does the porcini have under its cap?
86673.e: The porcini has no gills under its cap. Instead there are lots of fine tubes that look like a sponge.
86673.m: Under the porcini's cap there is a sponge of tubes.

86674.q: Is the porcini a good edible mushroom?
a: No, it is far too hard
No, only animals can eat it
86674.e: The porcini is one of the most popular edible mushrooms. Still, you should always have mushrooms you pick checked.
86674.m: The porcini is a very popular edible mushroom.

86675.q: What does the stem of the porcini look like?
86675.e: The stem of the porcini is thick and often bulging. It has a fine pale net pattern on it.
86675.m: The porcini stands on a thick stem.

86676.q: What colour is the flesh of the porcini when you cut it open?
86676.e: The flesh of the porcini is white. It does not change colour when you cut it.

86677.q: Under which trees do you often find porcini?
86677.e: The porcini lives together with forest trees such as spruces and beeches. It swaps nutrients with their roots.
86677.m: Porcini grow in the forest near spruces and beeches.

86678.q: What other name does the porcini have?
86678.e: The porcini is also called the king bolete. The name shows how highly prized it is.
86678.m: The porcini is also called the king bolete.

86679.q: What do people in Switzerland often call the chanterelle?
86679.e: In Switzerland the chanterelle is usually called Eierschwamm or Eierschwämmli, which means egg mushroom. The name comes from its egg-yolk yellow colour.
86679.m: In Switzerland the chanterelle is called Eierschwämmli.

86680.q: What does a fresh chanterelle smell of?
86680.e: Fresh chanterelles have a delicate, fruity smell. Many people think of apricots.
86680.m: The chanterelle smells delicately of apricots.

86681.q: What does the chanterelle have under its cap?
86681.e: The chanterelle has thick, forked ridges under its cap. They run a long way down the stem.
86681.m: There are ridges under the chanterelle's cap.

86682.q: What shape is the cap of an older chanterelle?
86682.e: On an older chanterelle the cap becomes deep in the middle. So it looks like a funnel.
86682.m: An older chanterelle has a cap like a funnel.

86683.q: Can you simply grow chanterelles in the garden?
a: No, they grow almost only in the wild
86683.e: Chanterelles need living forest trees as partners. That is why they are almost only picked in the forest.
86683.m: Chanterelles grow wild in the forest.

86684.q: Which plants does the chanterelle live together with?
86684.e: The chanterelle is linked to the roots of trees such as spruces, beeches and oaks. They help each other.
86684.m: The chanterelle and the forest trees are partners.

86685.q: What is the right way to eat chanterelles?
86685.e: Wild mushrooms should be heated well. Chanterelles are usually fried in a pan.
86685.m: Wild mushrooms are cooked well before eating.

86686.q: Which mushroom is sold most often in shops?
86686.e: Button mushrooms are grown in huge quantities. That is why you can buy them in almost every shop.
86686.m: You can buy button mushrooms in almost every shop.

86687.q: What colour are the gills of a young cultivated button mushroom?
86687.e: Young button mushrooms have pale pink gills. Later they get darker and darker.
86687.m: Young button mushrooms have pink gills.

86688.q: What colour are the gills of an old button mushroom?
86688.e: As the mushroom gets older, the spores turn the gills dark brown. This is normal for button mushrooms.
86688.m: Old button mushrooms have dark gills.

86689.q: Where are cultivated button mushrooms grown?
86689.e: Cultivated button mushrooms grow in dark, damp sheds. They stand there on a special compost.
86689.m: Cultivated button mushrooms grow in sheds on compost.

86690.q: In which colours can you buy cultivated button mushrooms?
86690.e: In the shop you can find white and brown mushrooms. The brown ones are often called chestnut mushrooms.
86690.m: Button mushrooms come in white or brown.

86691.q: Which wild mushroom often grows in pastures with cows and horses?
86691.e: The field mushroom grows in fertilised meadows and pastures. There is lots of dung from cows and horses there.
86691.m: The field mushroom grows in pastures.

86692.q: Which deadly poisonous mushroom can be mistaken for young button mushrooms?
86692.e: Young button mushrooms and death caps look alike. That is why you have to be very careful when picking them.
86692.m: Anyone who picks mushrooms must know the death cap.

86693.q: What does the French word “champignon” mean?
86693.e: In French, every mushroom is called a “champignon”. In German, the word only means one particular kind of mushroom.
86693.m: “Champignon” is the French word for mushroom.

86695.q: How dangerous is the death cap?
a: It is a good edible mushroom
86695.e: The death cap is one of the most poisonous mushrooms. Just one mushroom can kill a person.
86695.m: The death cap is deadly poisonous.

86696.q: Which organ does the poison of the death cap mainly destroy?
86696.e: The poison of the death cap mainly attacks the liver. It can be badly damaged.
86696.m: The poison of the death cap harms the liver.

86697.q: What colour is the cap of the death cap?
86697.e: Its cap is olive green to yellowish green. Sometimes, though, it is very pale.
86697.m: The death cap has a greenish cap.

86698.q: What does the death cap have at the bottom of its stem?
86698.e: At the bottom of the stem it has a thick bulb. It sits in a skin-like sac that is often hidden in the ground.
86698.m: The death cap has a bulb at the bottom of its stem.

86699.q: What colour is the death cap underneath its cap?
86699.e: Under its cap the death cap has lots of thin white gills. They always stay white, even when the mushroom is old.
86699.m: The death cap is white under its cap.

86700.q: Does cooking make the death cap harmless?
86700.e: The poison of the death cap can stand heat. Even cooking, frying or drying do not make it safe to eat.
86700.m: Cooking does not destroy the poison of the death cap.

86701.q: When do people often first notice that they have been poisoned by death caps?
86701.e: The first symptoms often only appear many hours after the meal. That is what makes this poisoning so dangerous.
86701.m: Mushroom poisoning often shows up late.

86703.q: What do you take to hospital if you think someone has mushroom poisoning?
a: Leftovers of the mushrooms that were eaten
86703.e: With leftovers of the mushrooms or the meal, experts can identify the mushroom. Then they know faster how to help.
86703.m: In mushroom poisoning, the leftover mushrooms help the doctors.

86704.q: What does the shape of a large parasol mushroom remind you of?
86704.e: The open cap of the parasol mushroom is flat and wide like a sunshade. “Parasol” is the French word for sunshade.
86704.m: The parasol mushroom looks like a sunshade.

86705.q: How big can the cap of a parasol mushroom get?
86705.e: The parasol is one of the biggest mushrooms in our forests. Its cap gets about as wide as a large plate.
86705.m: The parasol mushroom has a huge cap.

86706.q: What does the parasol mushroom have on its stem that you can slide?
86706.e: The parasol mushroom has a thick ring on its stem. You can slide it up and down the stem.
86706.m: The ring of the parasol mushroom can be moved.

86707.q: What does the stem of the parasol mushroom look like?
a: Long with a brown snakeskin pattern
86707.e: The stem of the parasol mushroom is long and slender. It has a brown pattern that looks like snakeskin.
86707.m: The parasol mushroom has a long, patterned stem.

86709.q: Which part of the parasol mushroom do you eat?
86709.e: With the parasol mushroom you only eat the cap. The stem is hard and stringy.
86709.m: You eat the cap of the parasol mushroom.

86710.q: How is the cap of the parasol mushroom often cooked?
86710.e: You can coat the big, flat cap in breadcrumbs and fry it. That is why it is also called a mushroom schnitzel.
86710.m: The cap of the parasol mushroom is often fried like a schnitzel.

86711.q: Where does the parasol mushroom like to grow?
a: At the edges of woods and in clearings
86711.e: The parasol mushroom likes bright places. You find it at the edges of woods, in clearings and in meadows.
86711.m: The parasol mushroom likes bright woodland edges.

86712.e: Honey fungus grows in dense clumps on tree stumps and trees. Often dozens of mushrooms stand together.
86712.m: Honey fungus grows in clumps on wood.

86713.q: What colour is honey fungus usually?
86713.e: Honey fungus is honey yellow to brown. That is where its English name comes from.
86713.m: Honey fungus is honey yellow in colour.

86714.q: Can you eat honey fungus raw?
86714.e: Raw honey fungus is poisonous. It only becomes safe to eat when heated well, and even then not everyone can tolerate it.

86715.q: What can honey fungus do to trees?
86715.e: Honey fungus can attack living trees. The trees become ill and can die.
86715.m: Honey fungus can make trees ill.

86716.q: Where in Switzerland was a giant honey fungus discovered?
86716.e: Researchers found a giant honey fungus in the Swiss National Park in the Grisons. Its network of threads is several hundred metres across.
86716.m: A giant honey fungus lives in the National Park.

86717.q: What can wood with honey fungus threads in it do at night?
86717.e: Wood with honey fungus growing in it can glow faintly in the dark. It is called foxfire.
86717.m: Wood with honey fungus can glow in the dark.

86718.q: When in the year does honey fungus usually appear?
86718.e: Honey fungus grows mainly in autumn. Then you often find it in large amounts.
86718.m: Honey fungus is an autumn mushroom.

86719.q: What is special about a honey fungus in the USA?
a: It is one of the largest living things
86719.e: In the USA there is a honey fungus whose network of threads spreads through many square kilometres of ground. It is thought to be one of the largest living things on Earth.
86719.m: A honey fungus can grow enormous.

86720.q: Where does the hoof fungus grow?
86720.e: The hoof fungus grows right on the trunks of trees. It sits there like a shelf.
86720.m: The hoof fungus grows on tree trunks.

86721.q: What shape is the hoof fungus?
86721.e: The hoof fungus looks like a big horse's hoof. It has no stem.
86721.m: The hoof fungus looks like a horse's hoof.

86722.q: What did people use the hoof fungus for in the past?
86722.e: People made tinder from the inside of the fungus. With it they could catch a spark and start a fire.
86722.m: In the past people made fire with the hoof fungus.

86723.q: Which fungus did Ötzi the Iceman have with him over 5,000 years ago?
86723.e: Ötzi lived in the Alps in the Stone Age. Hoof fungus for making fire was found among his equipment.
86723.m: Even Ötzi carried hoof fungus with him.

86724.q: Can you eat the hoof fungus?
a: No, it is as hard as wood
86724.e: The hoof fungus is hard and tough like wood. It is not suitable for eating.
86724.m: The hoof fungus is too hard to eat.

86725.q: How long does a hoof fungus live?
86725.e: The hoof fungus grows for several years. Each year a new layer is added.
86725.m: The hoof fungus gets a bit bigger every year.

86726.q: On which trees does the hoof fungus grow especially often?
86726.e: The hoof fungus grows mainly on beeches and birches. Usually the trees are already weak or dead.
86726.m: The hoof fungus likes to grow on beeches and birches.

86727.q: What does the hoof fungus do to the wood of the tree?
a: It makes it soft and rotten
It makes it as hard as stone
86727.e: The hoof fungus breaks down the wood. It becomes soft and rotten, and the tree can snap.
86727.m: The hoof fungus makes wood rotten.

86729.q: What is the expert who checks picked mushrooms called?
86729.e: Mushroom inspectors have special training. They can tell poisonous and edible mushrooms apart.
86729.m: The mushroom inspector knows mushrooms very well.

86730.q: How should you bring mushrooms to be checked?
86730.e: For the check the whole mushroom is needed. The stem and its bulb also help to identify it.
86730.m: Bring mushrooms whole to be checked.

86731.q: What is the best thing to carry picked mushrooms in?
86731.e: In a basket the mushrooms get air and are not squashed. In a plastic bag they go off quickly.
86731.m: Collect mushrooms in an airy basket.

86732.q: Can you taste an unknown mushroom to test whether it is poisonous?
a: Yes, if animals have nibbled it
86732.e: Some mushrooms are deadly even in tiny amounts. Bite marks from animals do not show that a mushroom is edible either.
86732.m: Tasting is not a test for mushrooms.

86733.q: Why should you have mushrooms checked even if an app has identified them?
86733.e: An app only recognises mushrooms from a photo. It can mix up poisonous and edible mushrooms.
86733.m: An app does not replace a mushroom check.

86734.q: What rule applies to mushroom picking in many Swiss cantons?
a: You may only pick at night
You may only pick red mushrooms
86734.e: Many cantons only allow a certain amount of mushrooms per person per day. This way enough mushrooms stay in the forest.
86734.m: There are rules about how many mushrooms you may pick.

86735.q: How often should you have edible mushrooms checked before eating them?
86735.e: Any batch you pick could contain a poisonous mushroom. That is why you have the mushrooms checked every time.
86735.m: Have picked mushrooms checked every time.

86736.q: What is the network of fine threads that a fungus forms in the ground called?
86736.e: Most of a fungus lives hidden in the ground. This network of fine threads is called mycelium.
86736.m: The mycelium is the hidden part of the fungus.

86737.q: Is the mushroom we see in the forest the whole fungus?
a: Yes, that is the whole fungus
No, that is only its flower
86737.e: What we pick in the forest is only the fruiting body. Most of the fungus lives as a fine network in the ground.
86737.m: The mushroom you see is only a small part.

86738.q: What does the mycelium of many fungi do with dead leaves in the forest?
a: It breaks them down into soil
86738.e: The mycelium of many fungi breaks down dead leaves and wood. This creates new, fertile soil.
86738.m: Fungi turn dead leaves into new soil.

86739.q: How do many fungi and trees help each other?
a: They keep each other warm in winter
86739.e: The mycelium wraps around the tree roots. The fungus gives water and mineral salts, and the tree gives sugar.

86740.q: Where does the mycelium of a fungus grow?
a: In the ground or in wood
86740.e: The mycelium grows hidden in the ground or in wood. There it takes in food.
86740.m: The mycelium grows in the ground or in wood.

86741.e: When you turn over leaves, you often see fine white threads. That is usually the mycelium of a fungus.
86741.m: Mycelium often looks like white cotton wool.

86742.q: How long can a mycelium live?
86742.e: A mycelium can live for many years and sometimes even for centuries. New mushrooms grow from it every year.
86742.m: A mycelium can get very old.

86743.q: What happens to the mycelium when you carefully pick a mushroom?
86743.e: The mushroom you pick is only a small part. The mycelium in the ground lives on and makes new mushrooms.
86743.m: The mycelium lives on after picking.

86744.q: What are the gills of a mushroom?
86744.e: Many mushrooms have thin plates under their cap. These are called gills.
86744.m: Gills are thin plates under the cap.

86745.q: What forms on the gills of a mushroom?
86745.e: Tiny spores form on the gills. New fungi can grow from them.
86745.m: The spores grow on the gills.

86746.q: What are the spores of a fungus for?
a: So that new fungi can grow
So that the mushroom smells nice
So that the mushroom can swim
86746.e: Spores are to fungi roughly what seeds are to plants. A new fungus network can grow from them.

86747.q: How can you make the colour of the spores visible?
a: Put the cap on a piece of paper
86747.e: You put the cap gills down on a piece of paper. After a few hours you can see a print made of spore powder.
86747.m: A spore print shows the colour of the spores.

86748.q: Where are the gills of a mushroom?
a: At the bottom of the bulb
86748.e: The gills are on the underside of the cap. The spores fall down from there.
86748.m: The gills are under the cap.

86749.q: How are the gills arranged under the cap?
86749.e: The gills run out from the stem to the edge of the cap like rays. They look like the spokes of a bicycle wheel.
86749.m: Gills run outwards from the stem like spokes.

86750.q: What carries the tiny spores far away?
86750.e: Spores are so light that the wind carries them far away. This way fungi can grow in new places.
86750.m: The wind spreads the spores of fungi.

86751.q: Can you see a single spore with the naked eye?
a: Yes, it is as big as a pea
Yes, it is as big as an egg
86751.e: A single spore is far too small for our eyes. Only lots of spores together can be seen as a powder.
86751.m: You can only see single spores under a microscope.

86752.q: Why do the mushrooms in a fairy ring stand in a circle?
a: The fungus grows underground in all directions
Animals arrange the mushrooms like that
The wind arranges them like that
86752.e: Underground, the fungus grows like a fine net from one point outwards in all directions. The mushrooms come up at the outer edge.
86752.m: Underground, the fungus grows outwards in a circle.

86753.q: Where can you see fairy rings especially well?
86753.e: In a meadow or on a lawn the circle of mushrooms is easy to spot. There are also fairy rings in forests.
86753.m: Fairy rings are easy to see in meadows.

86754.q: What does the grass often look like in a fairy ring?
a: Darker green than next to it
86754.e: The fungus changes the soil. That is why the grass in the ring is often darker green or brown in places.
86754.m: In a fairy ring the grass often looks different.

86755.q: In German, rings of mushrooms are called witches' rings. What are they called in English?
86755.e: In English they are called fairy rings. In the past people said that fairies danced in a circle there at night.
86755.m: A witches' ring is also called a fairy ring.

86756.q: How old can some fairy rings be?
86756.e: Some fairy rings are very big and have been growing for centuries. Their mycelium is just as old.
86756.m: Some fairy rings are hundreds of years old.

86757.q: What is the science that studies how animals behave called?
86757.e: Animal behaviour science, also called ethology, observes how animals live, eat and get along with each other.
86757.m: Animal behaviour science studies how animals behave.

86758.q: What do you call animals that are mainly out and about at night?
86758.e: Nocturnal animals sleep during the day and look for food in the dark. They include owls, bats and badgers.
86758.m: Nocturnal animals are out and about in the dark.

86759.q: Which scientist did young geese follow as if he were their mother?
86759.e: Konrad Lorenz raised young greylag geese. The goslings followed him everywhere, because he was the first thing they saw.
86759.m: Konrad Lorenz was like a mother to young geese.

86760.q: What is it called when goslings follow the first creature they see?
86760.e: Newly hatched goslings remember the first moving creature they see. This kind of learning is called imprinting.
86760.m: Goslings are imprinted on their mother.

86761.q: What is especially important when watching wild animals?
a: Being quiet and keeping your distance
86761.e: Wild animals are shy and run away from noise. If you are quiet and keep your distance, you see more and do not disturb the animals.
86761.m: If you want to watch animals, stay quiet and keep your distance.

86762.q: What can you use to see animals well from far away?
86762.e: Binoculars bring faraway things close. That way you can watch animals without disturbing them.
86762.m: With binoculars you can see animals from far away.

86763.q: What do scientists write down for every animal observation?
86763.e: With the date, time and place, observations can be compared later. That shows when and where animals are about.
86763.m: Every observation needs a date, time and place.

86764.q: What is the raised seat at the edge of the forest from which people watch wild animals called?
86764.e: From a high seat you can see far across the meadow. The animals notice a person up there less.
86764.m: From a high seat you can watch wild animals well.

86765.q: Where can you see animal tracks especially well?
86765.e: In soft snow and mud, animals’ feet leave clear prints. That is where tracks are easy to read.
86765.m: Animal tracks are especially easy to see in snow.

86766.q: Which animal leaves prints of split hooves?
86766.e: The roe deer is an even-toed hoofed animal. Its print shows two pointed halves of a hoof.
86766.m: The roe deer leaves prints of two hoof halves.

86767.q: How many toe pads can you see in a fox’s footprint?
86767.e: In a fox’s footprint you can see four toe pads and one large pad. Claws can often be seen too.
86767.m: The fox leaves prints with four toes.

86768.q: Why can you usually not see any claws in a cat’s tracks?
86768.e: Cats pull their claws in when they walk. With dogs and foxes, on the other hand, you can often see the claws.
86768.m: Claws are missing in cat tracks.

86769.q: Which animal leaves behind gnawed cones with frayed edges?
86769.e: The squirrel tears off the scales to get to the seeds. What is left is a frayed core.
86769.m: Frayed cones give the squirrel away.

86770.q: What are the droppings of wild animals called?
86770.e: Hunters and foresters call the droppings of wild animals scat. They show which animal has been there.
86770.m: Scat is the droppings of wild animals.

86771.e: Owls cough up the hair and bones of their prey as balls. In owl pellets you often find tiny mouse bones.
86771.m: Owl pellets are balls coughed up by owls.

86773.q: What is special about the tracks of a hopping hare?
a: The back paws land in front
86773.e: When it hops, the hare swings its long back legs past its front legs. That is why the big prints are at the front.
86773.m: With a hare, the back paw prints are at the front.

86774.q: When does a wildlife camera take a picture?
a: Only when you press a button
86774.e: A wildlife camera has a motion sensor. When an animal moves, it goes off automatically.
86774.m: A wildlife camera takes a photo when something moves.

86775.q: What does a wildlife camera use to take pictures at night without dazzling the animals?
86775.e: Infrared light can hardly be seen by most animals or by us. But the camera can still take pictures with it.
86775.m: At night, a wildlife camera uses infrared light.

86776.q: What do the night pictures from a wildlife camera usually look like?
86776.e: Infrared light makes pictures without colours. That is why night pictures are usually black and white.
86776.m: Night pictures from a wildlife camera are usually black and white.

86777.q: Why does a wildlife camera often have a green and brown pattern?
a: So that it is well camouflaged
86777.e: With a pattern like bark and leaves, the camera hardly stands out in the forest. That also means it gets stolen less often.
86777.m: A wildlife camera is well camouflaged in the forest.

86778.q: Where is a wildlife camera usually attached?
86778.e: The camera is strapped to a tree trunk, often at knee height. It points at an animal trail or a feeding place.
86778.m: Wildlife cameras usually hang on tree trunks.

86779.q: Where does a wildlife camera in the forest get its power from?
86779.e: There are no plug sockets in the forest. That is why wildlife cameras work with batteries or rechargeable batteries.

86780.q: What must you pay attention to when setting up a wildlife camera?
86780.e: People must not simply be filmed without knowing it. That is why the camera is not pointed at paths.
86780.m: A wildlife camera should film animals, not people.

86781.q: Why are wildlife cameras good for research?
86781.e: The camera works on its own, even for days. That is why the animals behave quite naturally.
86781.m: With wildlife cameras you can see animals without disturbing them.

86782.q: Which spotted predator in Switzerland can be recognised on wildlife camera photos by the pattern of its fur?
86782.e: Every lynx has its own pattern of spots in its fur. On photos, individual animals can therefore be recognised and counted.
86782.m: Lynxes are recognised on photos by their spots.

86783.q: Which ant lays the eggs in an ant colony?
86783.e: In an ant colony, the queen lays the eggs. The other ants take care of everything else.
86783.m: The queen lays the eggs in an ant colony.

86784.q: What are most of the ants in an ant colony called?
86784.e: Most ants are workers. They gather food, build and look after the young.
86784.m: The workers do almost all the jobs.

86785.q: How do ants find the way to a source of food?
86785.e: Ants lay a scent trail on the ground. Other ants follow this trail to the food.

86786.q: What does the red wood ant build in Swiss forests?
a: A clay nest on a tree
86786.e: The red wood ant builds big mounds in the forest. Underneath, the nest lies deep in the ground.
86786.m: The red wood ant builds mounds in the forest.

86787.q: What do wood ants build their mound from?
86787.e: Wood ants carry needles, small twigs and bits of resin together. Underneath, the nest lies deep in the ground.
86787.m: Ant mounds are made of needles and small twigs.

86788.q: What do ants get from aphids?
86788.e: Aphids give off a sweet juice called honeydew. Ants drink it and protect the aphids in return.
86788.m: Ants love the sweet honeydew of aphids.

86789.q: How do wood ants defend themselves against enemies?
86789.e: When in danger, wood ants squirt formic acid from the end of their body. It stings and drives enemies away.
86789.m: Wood ants defend themselves with formic acid.

86790.q: How much can an ant carry?
86790.e: Ants are very strong for their size. They drag things that are much heavier than themselves.
86790.m: Ants carry much more than they weigh themselves.

86791.q: Why do honeybees dance in the hive?
a: They show where there is food
86791.e: A bee that has found lots of flowers dances on the honeycomb. That way the others find out where the food is.
86791.m: With their dance, bees show the way to food.

86792.q: Which scientist worked out the dance language of bees?
86792.e: Karl von Frisch studied honeybees for decades. He found out what their dances mean.
86792.m: Karl von Frisch understood the language of bees.

86793.q: Which prize did Karl von Frisch receive for his research on bees?
86793.e: Karl von Frisch received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1973. He shared it with Konrad Lorenz and Nikolaas Tinbergen.
86793.m: Karl von Frisch received the Nobel Prize.

86794.q: Which dance does a bee do when the food is very close?
86794.e: When the food is close, the bee runs in small circles. This is called the round dance.
86794.m: The round dance means the food is close.

86795.q: Which dance does a bee do when the food is far away?
86795.e: When the food is far away, the bee runs in a figure of eight and waggles its body in between. This is called the waggle dance.
86795.m: The waggle dance shows food that is far away.

a: On the honeycombs in the hive
86796.e: The bees dance on the honeycombs in the dark hive. The other bees feel the dance with their antennae.
86796.m: Bees dance on the honeycombs in the hive.

86797.q: What do bees use to show the direction in the waggle dance?
86797.e: The direction of the dance shows the angle between the food and the sun. That way the other bees find the way.
86797.m: Bees use the sun to guide them in their dance.

86798.q: How do other bees know which flowers the dancer has found?
a: From the scent she brings with her
From the colour of her wings
86798.e: The dancing bee carries the scent of the flowers on her. The other bees smell it with their antennae.
86798.m: The scent of the flowers shows which ones are meant.

86799.q: Which animal in the Alps really hibernates?
86799.e: The marmot sleeps all winter in its burrow. Roe deer, foxes and chamois stay awake in winter.
86799.m: The marmot hibernates for a long time.

86800.q: What happens to an animal’s body temperature during hibernation?
86800.e: During hibernation, the body cools down a lot. The heart and breathing also become very slow.
86800.m: During hibernation the body cools down a lot.

86801.q: Roughly how long does a marmot sleep in winter?
86801.e: The marmot usually sleeps from October to April. That is about half a year.
86801.m: The marmot sleeps through half the year.

86802.q: What does an animal live on during hibernation?
86802.e: Before winter, the animals eat until they have a thick layer of fat. They live on it while they sleep.
86802.m: During hibernation, animals live on their fat.

86803.q: What does the squirrel do in winter?
86803.e: The squirrel sleeps a lot in winter, but often wakes up. Then it eats from its stores.
86803.m: The squirrel has a winter rest but does not hibernate.

86804.q: What is the state of frogs in the cold winter called?
86804.e: Frogs cannot keep their own body warm. When it is cold, they become stiff and stop moving.

86805.q: Why should you not wake an animal that is hibernating?
a: Waking up uses a lot of energy
86805.e: When it wakes up, the animal has to warm up. That uses up a lot of its fat store, which it may then be missing in spring.
86805.m: Leave a hibernating animal in peace.

86806.q: Which animal is called “Siebenschläfer” (seven sleeper) in German because of its long hibernation?
86806.e: The edible dormouse sleeps for about seven months. That is where its German name comes from.
86806.m: The edible dormouse sleeps for about seven months.

86807.q: Which flying animal hibernates in caves and cellars?
86807.e: Bats find no insects in winter. That is why they hang asleep in caves, tunnels or cellars.

86808.q: Which hare in the Alps gets white fur in winter?
86808.e: The mountain hare changes its fur in autumn. In its white winter coat, it can hardly be seen in the snow.
86808.m: The mountain hare is white in winter.

86809.q: Which bird of the Alps turns white in winter?
86809.e: The rock ptarmigan has white feathers in winter. That way it is well hidden in the snow.
86809.m: The rock ptarmigan is white in winter.

86810.q: Which animal can change the colour of its skin?
86810.e: The chameleon can change its colour. It also uses this to show its mood.

86811.q: Why do young roe deer have white spots on their fur?
86811.e: The fawn often lies alone in long grass. The spots look like patches of sunlight and hide it.

86812.q: Which insect looks like a thin twig?
86812.e: The stick insect is long, thin and brown or green. Among twigs you can hardly see it.
86812.m: The stick insect looks like a twig.

86813.q: Which insect looks like a green leaf?
86813.e: The leaf insect has a flat, green body with veins. It looks like a real leaf.
86813.m: The leaf insect is camouflaged as a leaf.

86814.q: Why is camouflage useful for an animal?
a: It is not spotted so easily
86814.e: Well camouflaged animals are hard for enemies to see. Hunters such as foxes can also use it to creep up on their prey.

86815.q: Which small member of the weasel family turns white in winter, except for the black tip of its tail?
86815.e: The stoat is brown in summer and white in winter. Only the tip of its tail always stays black.
86815.m: The stoat always has a black tail tip.

86816.q: Which food do tits especially like at the bird table?
86816.e: Tits like to peck fatty seeds such as sunflower seeds. They give a lot of energy in winter.

86817.q: Why should you not give birds bread?
a: It swells up in the stomach
86817.e: Bread swells up in a bird’s stomach and goes mouldy quickly. It fills the birds up, but does not keep them healthy.
86817.m: Bread does not belong on the bird table.

86818.q: Why must a bird table be kept clean?
a: So that the birds do not get ill
86818.e: Otherwise droppings and mould end up in the food. This can spread diseases among the birds.
86818.m: A clean bird table protects birds from disease.

86819.q: Where is the best place to put a bird table?
a: Raised up with a good view
Right on the ground in the bushes
Right next to the cat basket
In the middle of the road
86819.e: A high bird table with a clear view protects against cats. The birds see enemies coming early.
86819.m: A bird table should be raised and easy to see from.

86820.q: Which bird at the bird table has a yellow belly and a black head?
86820.e: The great tit has a yellow belly with a black stripe. Its head is black with white cheeks.
86820.m: The great tit has a yellow belly.

86821.q: Which small bird has an orange-red breast?
86821.e: You can recognise the robin by its orange-red breast and throat. It likes to feed on the ground.
86821.m: The robin has an orange-red breast.

86822.q: Which bird is completely black and has a yellow beak?
86822.e: The male blackbird is black with a yellow beak. The female is dark brown.
86822.m: The male blackbird is black with a yellow beak.

86823.q: Why is a feeder tube better than an open feeding tray?
a: The birds cannot step in the food
86823.e: In a feeder tube the food stays dry and clean. The birds cannot get into it with their feet and droppings.
86823.m: In a feeder tube, bird food stays clean.

86824.q: When is the hedgehog out and about?
86824.e: The hedgehog is a nocturnal animal. During the day it sleeps in a hiding place.
86824.m: The hedgehog looks for food at night.

86825.q: What does the hedgehog like to eat best?
86825.e: The hedgehog mainly eats insects such as beetles and caterpillars. Earthworms are on its menu too.
86825.m: The hedgehog likes eating beetles and caterpillars.

86826.q: Should you give a hedgehog milk?
a: Yes, it is its favourite food
86826.e: Hedgehogs cannot digest cow’s milk. It gives them diarrhoea. A bowl of fresh water is better.

86827.q: What can you do for hedgehogs in the garden?
86827.e: In a pile of leaves, the hedgehog finds a hiding place and food. It can also spend the winter there.
86827.m: A pile of leaves is a good hiding place for a hedgehog.

86828.q: Roughly how many spines does an adult hedgehog have?
86828.e: An adult hedgehog has about 6,000 to 8,000 spines. They protect it from enemies.
86828.m: The hedgehog has thousands of spines.

86829.q: What does a hedgehog do when it is in danger?
a: It rolls up into a ball
86829.e: When in danger, the hedgehog rolls itself up. Then all its spines point outwards.
86829.m: When in danger, the hedgehog rolls into a prickly ball.

86830.q: What is dangerous for hedgehogs in the garden at night?
86830.e: Hedgehogs are out at night and do not run away from machines. Robot lawnmowers can injure them badly.
86830.m: Robot lawnmowers should not run at night.

86831.q: Where are a Roman snail’s eyes?
86831.e: The eyes are at the tips of the long tentacles. When touched, the snail pulls its tentacles in.
86831.m: Snails have their eyes on their long tentacles.

86832.q: What does a snail need its slime for?
86832.e: The snail glides over the ground on its slime. The slime also protects its foot from sharp stones.
86832.m: The snail glides on its slime.

86833.q: In what kind of weather are snails especially active?
86833.e: Snails dry out easily in the sun. That is why they come out mainly when it rains and in the evening.
86833.m: After the rain, the snails come out.

86834.q: What do you call snails without a shell?
86834.e: Snails without a shell are called slugs. The large red slug is a well-known slug.

86835.q: What does a snail use to eat its food?
86835.e: Snails have a rasping tongue with lots of tiny teeth. They use it to scrape at leaves.
86835.m: The snail eats with a rasping tongue.

86836.q: What do you see if a snail crawls over a pane of glass and you look from below?
86836.e: The snail moves with waves of muscle on the underside of its foot. Through the glass you can see these waves clearly.
86836.m: A snail crawls with waves on its foot.

86837.e: The earthworm eats withered leaves and soil. It turns them into valuable humus.

86838.q: Why is the earthworm useful for the garden?
86838.e: Earthworms dig tunnels in the soil. That way air and water get to the plants’ roots.

a: No, it senses light with its skin
Yes, but only on its tail
86839.e: The earthworm has no eyes. But with its skin it can sense whether it is light or dark.
86839.m: The earthworm senses light with its skin.

86840.e: The earthworm breathes through its damp skin. That is why it must not dry out.
86840.m: The earthworm breathes through its skin.

86841.q: What does the earthworm use to hold on in its burrow?
86841.e: The earthworm has tiny bristles on the rings of its body. It uses them to hold on in the soil.
86841.m: The earthworm holds on with bristles.

86842.q: When does the earthworm pull leaves into its burrow?
86842.e: At night the earthworm comes up to the surface. It pulls leaves into its burrow to eat them.
86842.m: At night the earthworm pulls leaves into the ground.

86843.q: Which bird often pulls earthworms out of the lawn?
86843.e: The blackbird hops across the lawn and listens. Then it pulls an earthworm out of the ground with its beak.
86843.m: The blackbird hunts earthworms on the lawn.

86844.q: Does an earthworm cut in two always become two worms?
86844.e: An earthworm cut in two often dies. Sometimes only the front part can survive.
86844.m: Never cut an earthworm in two.

86845.q: Which bird calls out its own name?
86845.e: The cuckoo clearly calls “cuckoo”. That is how it got its name.
86845.m: The cuckoo calls its own name.

86846.q: Which bird calls “hoo-hoo” in the forest at night?
86846.e: The tawny owl is an owl. Its call can be heard clearly in the forest at night.
86846.m: The tawny owl calls in the forest at night.

86847.q: Which animal in the Alps gives a warning with a loud whistle?
86847.e: Marmots whistle loudly when an eagle or a fox comes. Then they all run quickly into their burrow.
86847.m: The marmot warns with a whistle.

86848.q: Which animals croak at the pond in spring?
86848.e: In spring the frogs croak at the pond. Some have vocal sacs that make their call louder.

86849.q: How does a field cricket chirp?
86849.e: The field cricket rubs its front wings against each other. That makes the well-known chirping sound.
86849.m: The cricket chirps with its wings.

86850.q: When do birds sing especially a lot in spring?
86850.e: Many birds start singing even before sunrise. This is called the dawn chorus.
86850.m: Birds sing most early in the morning.

86851.q: Why can we not hear the calls bats use to find their way?
a: They are too high for us
They are too quiet for anyone
They are too low for us
86851.e: Bats call in ultrasound. These sounds are too high for the human ear.

86852.q: Which wild animal makes barking sounds when it is in danger?
86852.e: A frightened roe deer gives short, barking sounds. This is called barking.
86852.m: A frightened roe deer can bark.

86853.q: What does the heart muscle do with every heartbeat?
86853.e: With every beat, the heart muscle contracts. In doing so it pushes blood out of the heart into the blood vessels.
86853.m: With every heartbeat, the heart muscle contracts.

86854.q: Which emergency number do you call in Switzerland if a person’s heart stops beating?
86854.e: In Switzerland, the number 144 calls the ambulance service. 117 is the police and 118 is the fire brigade.
86854.m: In a heart emergency in Switzerland, you call 144.

86855.q: Roughly how many times does an adult’s heart beat in a day?
86855.e: The heart beats many times every minute, day and night. Over 24 hours that adds up to about 100,000 beats.
86855.m: The heart beats about 100,000 times a day.

86856.q: Does the heart take a break at night?
86856.e: The heart always has to pump blood, even during sleep. It only takes a tiny rest between two beats.
86856.m: The heart beats day and night.

86857.q: When does your heart beat more slowly than when running?
86857.e: During sleep the body needs little energy. That is why the heart can beat calmly and slowly.
86857.m: During sleep, the heart beats slowly.

86858.q: Do you have to tell your heart to beat?
86858.e: The heart has its own pacemaker. It beats by itself without us having to think about it.
86858.m: The heart beats all by itself.

86859.q: Roughly how many times does a heart beat in a long life?
86859.e: The heart beats all life long without a break. In 80 years that adds up to about three billion beats.
86859.m: In a lifetime, the heart beats billions of times.

86860.q: What is the test called that records the heart’s electrical signals as a zigzag line?
86860.e: ECG stands for electrocardiogram. Small sticky pads on the skin measure the heart’s electrical signals.
86860.m: An ECG records the heart’s electrical signals.

86861.q: What helps the heart stay strong and healthy?
86861.e: The heart is a muscle. Like other muscles, it gets stronger through exercise and sport.

86862.q: What does blood bring to all parts of the body?
86862.e: The heart pumps blood through the body. The blood delivers oxygen and nutrients to every cell.
86862.m: Blood brings oxygen and nutrients into the body.

86863.q: What do you feel when you take your pulse?
a: The heartbeat in a blood vessel
86863.e: With every heartbeat, blood is pushed into the blood vessels. You feel this push in certain places as your pulse.
86863.m: The pulse is the heartbeat you feel in a blood vessel.

86864.q: In which unit is the pulse given?
86864.e: For the pulse, you count how many times the heart beats in one minute. That is why it is given in beats per minute.
86864.m: The pulse is given in beats per minute.

86865.q: Where on the neck do you feel your pulse?
a: On the side of the neck
At the back of the neck
In the middle under the chin
86865.e: On the side of the neck, next to the voice box, there is a large blood vessel. You can feel the pulse strongly there.
86865.m: You feel the pulse on the side of the neck.

86866.q: Which fingers are best for taking your pulse?
86866.e: You place your index and middle fingers gently on the blood vessel. That way you can feel the pulse clearly.
86866.m: Take your pulse with your index and middle fingers.

86867.q: Why do you not take a pulse with your thumb?
a: The thumb has a pulse of its own
86867.e: You can feel your own pulse quite strongly in your thumb. Then you do not know which pulse you are counting.
86867.m: You do not take a pulse with your thumb because it has its own pulse.

86868.q: You count 20 beats in 15 seconds. How many is that in a minute?
86868.e: A minute has 60 seconds, which is 4 times 15 seconds. So you work out 20 times 4, which makes 80.
86868.m: Beats in 15 seconds times 4 give the pulse per minute.

86869.q: You count 45 beats in 30 seconds. How many is that in a minute?
86869.e: A minute is twice as long as 30 seconds. So you work out 45 times 2, which makes 90.
86869.m: Beats in 30 seconds times 2 give the pulse per minute.

86870.q: What do you need to count your pulse accurately?
86870.e: The pulse is given in beats per minute. With a watch you measure how long you are counting.
86870.m: To count your pulse, you need a watch.

86871.q: What happens to your pulse when you climb stairs quickly?
86871.e: Climbing stairs is hard work for the leg muscles. They need more blood, so the pulse goes up.
86871.m: With effort, the pulse gets faster.

86872.q: What does the doctor need a stethoscope for?
a: For listening to the heart and lungs
86872.e: With a stethoscope, the doctor listens to sounds in the body. That way she checks whether the heart and lungs are working well.
86872.m: You listen to the heart and lungs with a stethoscope.

86873.q: Where do you put the two arms of a stethoscope?
86873.e: The arms have small earpieces. That way the sounds from the body go straight into the ears.
86873.m: You put the arms of the stethoscope in your ears.

86874.q: Where does the doctor put the round part of the stethoscope?
a: On the sole of the foot
86874.e: The doctor puts the round part on the chest or back. That way she can hear the heart and lungs.
86874.m: The stethoscope goes on the chest or back.

86875.q: Which country did the doctor who invented the stethoscope come from?
86875.e: The French doctor René Laennec invented the stethoscope in 1816. Before that, doctors put their ear directly on the chest.
86875.m: The stethoscope was invented in France.

86876.q: What did René Laennec make his stethoscope from, after first trying rolled-up paper?
86876.e: Laennec first rolled a sheet of paper into a tube. Then he made a tube out of wood. Tubes for both ears only came later.
86876.m: Laennec’s stethoscope was a wooden tube.

86877.q: What does the doctor hear when she listens to the lungs with a stethoscope?
a: The air flowing in and out
86877.e: When you breathe, air flows into the lungs and out again. This makes a soft rushing sound that you can hear with a stethoscope.
86877.m: With a stethoscope you hear the breathing in the lungs.

86878.q: Why can you hear quiet sounds in the body well with a stethoscope?
a: It carries them straight to the ears
86878.e: The stethoscope picks up the sounds and carries them through the tubes. Disturbing sounds from outside are blocked out.
86878.m: The stethoscope carries sounds from the body to the ears.

86879.q: Where do doctors often wear their stethoscope when they are not using it?
86879.e: Around the neck, the stethoscope is quickly to hand. That is why you often see doctors wearing it like that.
86879.m: The stethoscope often hangs around the neck.

86880.q: When do you feel your heart pounding especially strongly?
86880.e: After running, the heart works hard and fast. Then you feel it pounding in your chest.
86880.m: After running, the heart pounds hard.

86881.q: Why does the heart beat faster during sport?
86881.e: Working muscles need a lot of oxygen. So the heart pumps more blood to them, faster.
86881.m: During sport, the body needs more oxygen.

86882.q: When can your heart suddenly pound even without sport?
86882.e: With a fright, the body gets ready to react quickly. The heart beats faster and harder.
86882.m: With a fright, the heart pounds.

86883.q: You are nervous before performing at school. What does your heart often do?
86883.e: Excitement affects the body in a similar way to effort. The heart beats faster, which is completely normal.
86883.m: When you are excited, the heart beats faster.

86884.q: What helps when your heart is pounding with excitement?
a: Holding your breath for a long time
86884.e: Slow, deep breathing calms the body. This also makes the heartbeat calmer again.

86885.q: What happens to the pounding of your heart when you rest after sport?
86885.e: During the break, the muscles need less oxygen. The heart then gradually beats more calmly again.
86885.m: After sport, the heart calms down again.

86886.q: Which substance in the body makes the heart beat faster when you get a fright?
86886.e: With fear or a fright, the body releases adrenaline. This messenger substance makes the heart beat faster.
86886.m: Adrenaline makes the heart beat faster when you get a fright.

86887.q: Where do you usually feel your heart pounding?
86887.e: The heart is in the chest. When it beats hard, you feel the pounding most clearly there.
86887.m: You feel your heart pounding in your chest.

86888.e: Blood vessels are tubes throughout the body. In them, blood flows away from the heart and back again.
86888.m: Blood flows in the blood vessels.

86889.q: What are the tiniest blood vessels in the body called?
86889.e: The capillaries are so fine that they reach every cell.
86889.m: The smallest blood vessels are called capillaries.

86890.q: Why are the smallest blood vessels called capillaries, from the Latin word for hair?
a: They are thinner than a hair
They are only in the head
86890.e: These vessels are even thinner than a hair. You can only see them under a microscope.
86890.m: Capillaries are thinner than a hair.

86891.q: What forms when small blood vessels under the skin are injured by a knock?
86891.e: Blood leaks out of the injured vessels under the skin. You see this as a bruise, which slowly disappears again.
86891.m: A bruise comes from blood under the skin.

86892.q: Which three kinds of blood vessels are there?
86892.e: Arteries lead away from the heart, veins lead towards the heart. The capillaries connect the two.
86892.m: There are arteries, veins and capillaries.

86893.q: Why does your face go red during sport?
a: More blood flows into the skin
86893.e: During sport, the body gets warm. The blood vessels in the skin widen so that more blood can give off heat to the outside.
86893.m: During sport, more blood flows through the skin.

86894.q: Why do your fingers go pale when it is very cold?
86894.e: In the cold, the vessels in the fingers and toes narrow. That way the body loses less heat, but the skin goes pale.
86894.m: In the cold, the blood vessels get narrower.

86895.q: How does blood flow through the blood vessels?
a: Only once, then it is gone
86895.e: Blood flows from the heart into the body and back to the heart again. That is why we talk about the circulation of the blood.
86895.m: Blood flows round the body in a circuit.

86896.q: What is injured in a nosebleed?
a: Small blood vessels in the nose
86896.e: In the nose, many fine blood vessels lie just under the lining. They can burst easily, for example from nose picking or dry air.
86896.m: In a nosebleed, small vessels in the nose are injured.

86897.q: Where do the veins take the blood?
86897.e: Veins collect the blood in the body. They take it back to the heart.
86897.m: Veins carry blood to the heart.

86898.q: What do veins on the wrist look like through the skin?
86898.e: The veins lie just under the skin. Seen through the skin, they look bluish.
86898.m: Veins show bluish through the skin.

86899.q: Is the blood in the veins really blue?
86899.e: Blood is always red; in the veins it is dark red. Only through the skin do the veins look bluish.
86899.m: The blood in the veins is dark red.

86900.q: What do the veins in the legs have so that blood does not flow back?
86900.e: There are valves in the leg veins. Like doors, they only open in one direction, towards the heart.
86900.m: Vein valves only let blood flow towards the heart.

86901.q: What helps the blood in the leg veins flow upwards?
86901.e: When the leg muscles work, they press on the veins. That way the blood is pushed up to the heart.
86901.m: Movement helps the blood in the legs get back to the heart.

86902.q: When do the veins on the back of the hand stand out more?
a: When you hold your hand up
86902.e: If the hand hangs down, the blood in the veins flows back to the heart more slowly. The veins fill up and stand out.
86902.m: If your hand hangs down, the veins stand out.

86903.q: Where does the doctor usually take blood from when taking a blood sample?
a: From a vein in the crook of the elbow
From a bone in the leg
From the tip of the nose
86903.e: In the crook of the elbow, veins lie just under the skin. Blood can easily be taken there with a fine needle.
86903.m: Blood is usually taken from a vein in the crook of the elbow.

86904.q: Do veins have a thicker or thinner wall than arteries?
86904.e: In the veins, blood flows with little pressure. That is why their wall is thinner than the wall of the arteries.
86904.m: Veins have a thinner wall than arteries.

86905.q: Where do the arteries take the blood?
a: Away from the heart into the body
From the body back to the heart
86905.e: Arteries start at the heart. They carry blood away from the heart to all the organs.
86905.m: Arteries carry blood away from the heart.

86906.q: What is the largest artery in the body called?
86906.e: The aorta comes straight out of the heart. Many smaller arteries branch off from it into the whole body.
86906.m: The aorta is the largest artery.

86908.q: Where can you easily feel your heartbeat with your fingers?
a: On the sole of the foot
On the tip of the nose
86908.e: On the wrist, a blood vessel lies just under the skin. There you feel a throb with every heartbeat: the pulse.
86908.m: You can feel the pulse on your wrist.

86909.q: What is the large artery on the side of the neck called?
86909.e: The carotid artery brings blood to the head and brain. It is on the side of the neck.
86909.m: The carotid artery supplies the head with blood.

86910.q: What colour is the blood in most arteries?
86910.e: In most arteries, blood with lots of oxygen flows. Blood like this is bright red.
86910.m: Blood with lots of oxygen is bright red.

86911.q: Roughly how thick is an adult’s aorta?
86911.e: In adults, the aorta has a diameter of about 2.5 to 3.5 centimetres. That is about as thick as a garden hose.
86911.m: The aorta is about 3 centimetres thick.

86912.q: Why is an injury to a large artery very dangerous?
a: The skin turns blue straight away
86912.e: In arteries, the blood is under high pressure. With an injury, you therefore lose a lot of blood quickly.
86912.m: Blood spurts out strongly from an injured artery.

86913.q: What happens in the chambers of the heart before they pump blood out?
86913.e: First the chambers relax and fill with blood from the atria. Then they contract and push the blood out.
86913.m: The heart chambers fill with blood first.

86914.q: What kind of blood comes into the right chamber of the heart?
86914.e: Blood from the body flows back into the right half of the heart. It has already given its oxygen to the organs.
86914.m: Blood with little oxygen comes into the right heart chamber.

86915.q: What are the two upper spaces in the heart called?
86915.e: The atria are at the top of the heart. The blood collects there before it flows into the chambers.
86915.m: The upper spaces in the heart are called atria.

86916.q: Where does the right chamber of the heart pump the blood?
86916.e: The right chamber of the heart sends the blood to the lungs. There the blood takes in fresh oxygen.
86916.m: The right heart chamber pumps blood to the lungs.

86917.q: What do you hear with a stethoscope after a fast run?
a: The heart sounds come faster one after another
The heart sounds sound like music
The heart sounds only come every ten seconds
86917.e: After running, the heart beats faster. That is why you hear the heart sounds at shorter intervals.
86917.m: After running, you hear the heart sounds faster.

86918.q: Which chamber of the heart has the thicker muscle wall?
86918.e: The left chamber has to push the blood through the whole body. For that it needs more strength and a thicker wall.
86918.m: The left heart chamber has the thickest wall.

86919.q: What separates the left and right halves of the heart?
86919.e: In the middle of the heart there is a wall of muscle. It is called the septum and separates the two halves of the heart.
86919.m: The septum separates left and right in the heart.

86921.q: How well can you hear the heart sounds when listening through a thick jumper?
a: Much louder than on the skin
They then sound like a whistle
86921.e: The thick fabric muffles the quiet sounds and even makes rustling noises itself. That is why the doctor prefers to put the stethoscope directly on the skin.
86921.m: Heart sounds are heard best directly on the skin.

86922.q: How many heart sounds do you normally hear with a healthy heartbeat?
86922.e: With every heartbeat, you hear a first and a second heart sound. Then there is a short pause.
86922.m: With every heartbeat, you hear two heart sounds.

86923.q: Where do the heart sounds mainly come from?
86923.e: When the heart valves snap shut, a dull sound is made. The tensing of the heart muscle also contributes.
86923.m: The heart sounds come mainly from the heart valves closing.

86924.q: What does the doctor listen to your heart with?
86924.e: The stethoscope has two earpieces and a round head. When the doctor puts it on your chest, she hears the heart sounds.
86924.m: You listen to the heart with a stethoscope.

86925.q: Can you hear the heart sounds without a stethoscope too?
a: Yes, with your ear on the chest
86925.e: If you put your ear on another person’s chest, you can hear the heart sounds quietly. That is what doctors did before the stethoscope existed.
86925.m: With your ear on the chest, you can hear the heart sounds.

86926.q: Why must the room be quiet when listening to the heart sounds?
a: Because the heart sounds are quiet
Because otherwise the blood stops flowing
86926.e: Heart sounds are quiet noises. Noise in the room would drown them out.
86926.m: Heart sounds are heard best in a quiet room.

a: The pulse when you are completely calm
86927.e: The resting pulse is measured when you are not making any effort. It shows how fast the heart beats at rest.
86927.m: The resting pulse is the pulse at rest.

86928.q: When is the best time to measure your resting pulse?
a: In the morning after waking up
86928.e: In the morning in bed, the body is still completely relaxed. Then the pulse is at its calmest.
86928.m: Measure your resting pulse in the morning in bed.

86929.q: Roughly how high is the resting pulse of a healthy adult?
86929.e: In adults, the heart at rest usually beats 60 to 80 times a minute. That is about once a second.
86929.m: The resting pulse of adults is usually 60 to 80.

86930.q: Who usually has the fastest resting pulse?
86930.e: Newborn babies have a resting pulse of about 120 to 140 beats per minute. The older a child gets, the more slowly its heart beats at rest.
86930.m: Babies have the fastest resting pulse.

86931.q: Why do well-trained athletes often have a low resting pulse?
a: Their heart pumps more blood per beat
86931.e: Training makes the heart stronger. It pumps more blood with every beat and so needs to beat less often.
86931.m: A trained heart beats more slowly at rest.

86932.q: Which animal has a much faster pulse than humans?
86932.e: Small animals usually have a fast heartbeat. A mouse’s heart beats several hundred times a minute.
86932.m: The mouse has a very fast pulse.

86933.q: Which animal has a slower resting pulse than humans?
86933.e: Large animals usually have a slow heartbeat. An elephant’s heart beats about 30 times a minute at rest.
86933.m: The elephant has a slow pulse.

86934.q: What should you not do just before measuring your resting pulse?
86934.e: Movement makes the pulse faster. For the resting pulse you therefore have to keep still for a few minutes.
86934.m: Keep calm before measuring your resting pulse.

86935.q: Roughly how big is your heart?
86935.e: If you clench your hand into a fist, you can see roughly how big your own heart is.
86935.m: Your heart is about as big as your fist.

86936.q: Which way does the tip of the heart point?
86936.e: The heart sits at an angle in the chest. Its tip points down and to the left.
86936.m: The tip of the heart points down and to the left.

86937.q: Between which organs is the heart?
86937.e: The lungs are to the left and right of the heart. The left lung is a little smaller because the heart needs room.
86937.m: The heart is between the lungs.

86938.q: Roughly how much does an adult’s heart weigh?
86938.e: An adult heart weighs about 250 to 350 grams.
86938.m: An adult heart weighs about 300 grams.

86939.q: Does the heart grow as a child gets bigger?
a: Yes, it grows with the body
No, it stays the same size
86939.e: A bigger body needs more blood. That is why the heart grows too, until you are an adult.
86939.m: The heart grows along with the body.

86940.q: Does a real heart look like the heart symbol on a card?
86940.e: A real heart is shaped like a rounded cone with a point at the bottom. The drawn heart symbol is only a sign.
86940.m: A real heart looks different from the heart symbol.

86941.q: Which animal has the biggest heart?
86941.e: The blue whale is the largest animal on Earth. One blue whale heart that was measured weighed about 180 kilograms, as much as two or three adults.
86941.m: The blue whale has the biggest heart.

86942.q: What protects the heart from knocks from outside?
86942.e: The ribs, breastbone and spine together form the ribcage. It surrounds the heart like a protective cage.

86943.q: What does a blood pressure monitor measure?
a: How hard the blood presses in the blood vessels
86943.e: Blood presses against the walls of the blood vessels. A blood pressure monitor measures this pressure.
86943.m: A blood pressure monitor measures the pressure of the blood.

86944.q: What is the band called that is put around your arm when your blood pressure is measured?
