86944.e: The cuff is a band with an air cushion inside. It is wrapped around the arm and fastened tightly.
86944.m: A cuff is put around the arm to measure blood pressure.

86945.q: Where is the cuff usually put when measuring blood pressure?
86945.e: Blood pressure is usually measured on the upper arm, at about the height of the heart. Some devices measure at the wrist.
86945.m: Blood pressure is usually measured on the upper arm.

86946.q: What happens to the cuff during the measurement?
a: It is pumped up with air
86946.e: The cuff is pumped up with air and presses on the arm. Then the device slowly lets the air out again.
86946.m: The cuff is pumped up with air.

86947.q: How many numbers are given for blood pressure?
86947.e: One number shows the pressure when the heart pumps. The other shows the pressure between two heartbeats.
86947.m: Blood pressure is given as two numbers.

86948.q: In which unit is blood pressure given?
86948.e: Blood pressure monitors used to have a column of mercury. The unit is shortened to mmHg.
86948.m: Blood pressure is given in millimetres of mercury.

86949.q: Which blood pressure is roughly normal for adults?
86949.e: A blood pressure of about 120 over 80 is a good value for adults. Children usually have slightly lower blood pressure.
86949.m: Normal blood pressure is about 120 over 80.

86950.q: How should you behave while your blood pressure is being measured?
86950.e: Moving and talking change your blood pressure. That is why you sit still and relaxed.
86950.m: Sit still while your blood pressure is measured.

86951.q: Where in Switzerland can you have your blood pressure measured without a doctor's appointment?
86951.e: Many pharmacies in Switzerland offer blood pressure checks. The staff there can also explain the results.
86951.m: You can have your blood pressure measured at a pharmacy.

86952.q: Which value does an electronic blood pressure monitor often show as well?
86952.e: While measuring, the device feels the heartbeats in the arm. That is why it usually shows the pulse too.
86952.m: A blood pressure monitor often shows the pulse too.

86953.q: What do you need for something to move, shine or get warm?
86953.e: Without energy nothing happens: no car drives, no lamp shines and no oven gets warm.
86953.m: You need energy for movement, light and warmth.

86954.e: Energy is never lost. It only changes its form; for example, the energy from food becomes the movement of your muscles.
86954.m: Energy does not disappear, it is changed.

86956.q: In which unit does the electricity bill show how much energy was used?
86956.e: Electricity use is measured in kilowatt hours. The more kilowatt hours, the higher the bill.
86956.m: Electricity use is measured in kilowatt hours.

86957.q: Which appliance turns electricity mainly into heat?
86957.e: In a kettle, a heating element gets hot from the electricity. This heat brings the water to the boil.
86957.m: A kettle turns electricity into heat.

86958.q: Where does most of the electricity produced in Switzerland come from?
86958.e: In 2024, hydroelectric power stations on rivers and reservoirs supplied about 60 per cent of Swiss electricity. The mountains and plentiful water are ideal for this.
86958.m: In Switzerland most electricity comes from hydropower.

86959.q: Which energy does a wind turbine use?
86959.e: The wind turns the big blades of the wind turbine. A generator turns this rotation into electricity.
86959.m: A wind turbine makes electricity from wind.

86960.q: What is produced when you hit a drum hard?
86960.e: The hit makes the drumskin vibrate. We hear these vibrations as sound.
86960.m: A drum turns movement into sound.

86961.q: What is produced when you rub your hands together quickly?
86961.e: When you rub, movement energy turns into heat. That is why your hands get warm.

86962.q: What does a dynamo on a bike make from the turning of the wheel?
86962.e: The dynamo is turned by the wheel. It changes the movement into electricity, which makes the bike lamp shine.
86962.m: A dynamo turns movement into electricity.

86963.q: What happens to a rechargeable battery after many years of use?
a: It does not last as long
86963.e: Each time it is charged, a battery ages a little. After years it stores less energy and the device has to be charged more often.
86963.m: Old batteries do not last as long.

86964.q: What do you do when a tablet's battery is empty?
86964.e: Electricity flows into the battery through the charging cable. Afterwards, energy is stored again.

86965.q: Which device almost always has a built-in rechargeable battery?
86965.e: A mobile phone needs energy even when it is not plugged in. That is why it has a battery built in.
86965.m: A mobile phone has a battery.

86966.q: Where do you take old rechargeable and ordinary batteries in Switzerland?
a: Back to the shop, to the collection point
86966.e: In Switzerland, shops that sell batteries take old batteries back free of charge. That way the materials can be recycled.
86966.m: Old batteries belong in battery collection.

86967.q: Why do rechargeable batteries not belong in the normal rubbish?
a: They contain substances that harm the environment
86967.e: Batteries contain metals and other substances that can harm nature. Batteries in household rubbish can also start a fire.
86967.m: Batteries do not belong in the rubbish.

86968.q: What does the little battery symbol on a mobile phone show?
86968.e: The battery symbol shows how charged the battery is. If it is almost empty, you should charge the phone soon.
86968.m: The battery symbol shows how full the battery is.

86969.q: What gives the motor of an e-bike its energy?
86969.e: The e-bike's battery is charged at a socket. It supplies the electricity for the motor that helps you pedal.
86969.m: An e-bike runs on a battery.

86970.q: Where is it better not to leave a battery lying around?
a: In a hot car in the sun
86970.e: Great heat damages batteries. They can break or, in the worst case, catch fire.
86970.m: Batteries do not like great heat.

86971.q: Why should you not plug lots of extension sockets into each other?
a: They can overheat and catch fire
86971.e: If too much electricity flows through a socket, it gets hot. In the worst case a fire starts.
86971.m: Too many devices on one socket are dangerous.

86972.q: How many holes does a normal Swiss socket have?
86972.e: The Swiss socket has three holes. The middle one is for the earth, which protects against electric shocks.
86972.m: The Swiss socket has three holes.

86973.q: Why must you never put anything metal into a socket?
a: You can get an electric shock
86973.e: Metal conducts electricity very well. The electricity from the socket can then flow through your body, and that can kill.
86973.m: Never put anything metal into a socket.

86974.q: What is a child safety cover on a socket for?
a: So children cannot put anything in
86974.e: The child safety cover closes off the holes of the socket. Only a proper plug can open it.
86974.m: The safety cover protects young children from electricity.

86975.q: What do you do with a device whose cable is broken?
86975.e: With a broken cable you can touch the electricity. An adult or an expert must repair it first.
86975.m: Do not use devices with a broken cable.

86976.q: Which foreign plug also fits into a Swiss socket?
86976.e: The slim Europlug with two round pins fits into Swiss sockets. For many other plugs you need an adapter.
86976.m: The flat Europlug fits into Swiss sockets.

86977.q: Where does the electricity in the socket come from?
a: Through lines from a power station
From the air in the room
86977.e: Power stations produce electricity. It reaches every home through long power lines and cables.
86977.m: Electricity comes through lines from power stations.

86978.q: Which food gives energy quickly but harms your teeth in large amounts?
86978.e: Sugar goes into the blood quickly and gives fast energy. But it is also food for the bacteria that cause tooth decay.
86978.m: Sugar gives quick energy, but too much harms your teeth.

86979.q: What does your body need energy for even while you sleep?
86979.e: Even in your sleep you breathe and stay warm. For this the body needs energy all the time.
86979.m: The body needs energy even in sleep.

86980.q: In which unit is the energy shown on food packaging?
86980.e: Packaging shows the energy content in kilocalories, kcal for short, and also in kilojoules, kJ for short.
86980.m: The energy in food is given in kilocalories.

86981.q: Which food contains especially much energy?
86981.e: Nuts contain lots of fat, and fat supplies a great deal of energy. Cucumbers and lettuce, on the other hand, are almost all water.

86982.q: How much energy does pure water contain?
86982.e: Water has no calories. Even so, the body urgently needs it, for example for the blood.
86982.m: Water supplies no energy, but it is vital.

86983.q: How do you feel when you have not eaten for a long time?
86983.e: When the body lacks food, it has less energy. You get tired and find it hard to concentrate.
86983.m: Without food, the body lacks energy.

86984.q: Who needs more energy from food?
86984.e: When you play football, many muscles are working. For this the body uses much more energy than at rest.
86984.m: If you move a lot, you need more energy.

86985.q: Which nutrients in bread, pasta and potatoes give the body energy?
86985.e: Carbohydrates such as starch and sugar are important sources of energy. They are found in bread, pasta, rice and potatoes.

86986.q: What is a cooker called that cooks food using only sunlight?
86986.e: A solar cooker uses mirrors to gather sunlight onto a pot. This heats the food without electricity or fire.
86986.m: A solar cooker cooks with sunlight.

86987.q: What is a system that makes electricity from sunlight called?
86987.e: Photovoltaic means electricity from light. In Switzerland you can see such systems on more and more roofs.
86987.m: A photovoltaic system makes electricity from light.

86988.q: What do plants need sunlight for?
86988.e: Plants use sunlight, water and air to make their own sugar. This process is called photosynthesis.
86988.m: Plants make their food with sunlight.

86989.q: Why is it cooler in the shade than in the sun?
86989.e: Sunlight brings warmth with it. In the shade it is blocked, so it is cooler there.
86989.m: In the shade, the sun's warmth is missing.

86990.q: What can you do with solar collectors on the roof?
86990.e: In solar collectors, water flows through pipes. The sun warms it, for example for the shower.

86991.q: What dries the washing on the line without any electricity?
86991.e: The sun's warmth makes the water in the washing evaporate. The wind carries the damp air away.
86991.m: Sun and wind dry the washing for free.

86992.q: When does a solar system make the most electricity?
a: At midday under a clear sky
In the middle of the night
86992.e: The most electricity is made when lots of sunlight falls on the solar cells. That is at midday with a cloudless sky.
86992.m: Sunshine at midday gives the most solar power.

86993.q: Why must you never leave a magnifying glass lying on paper in the sun?
a: It focuses the light and can start a fire
86993.e: The magnifying glass gathers sunlight into a small bright spot. It gets so hot there that paper can burn.
86993.m: A magnifying glass can focus sunlight enough to start a fire.

86994.q: What does burning wood give off?
86994.e: When wood burns, the energy in it is released. It appears as heat and as the light of the flames.
86994.m: Burning wood gives off heat and light.

a: Wet wood burns badly and smokes
86995.e: Wet wood contains lots of water. This must evaporate first, so the wood burns badly and makes lots of smoke.

86996.q: About how long do you leave freshly split firewood to dry?
86996.e: Fresh wood contains lots of water. Stacked in an airy place, it dries in one to two years.
86996.m: Firewood must dry for one to two years.

86997.q: Where does the energy in wood originally come from?
86997.e: The tree used sunlight as it grew. This energy is stored in the wood and is released when it burns.

86998.q: What do people in Switzerland call an open fireplace in the living room?
86998.e: In Switzerland, an open fireplace is called a cheminée. The word comes from French.
86998.m: In Switzerland, an open fireplace is called a cheminée.

86999.e: Wood pellets are pressed from sawdust and wood shavings. They are burned in special stoves for heating.
86999.m: Wood pellets are made of pressed sawdust.

87000.q: Which tool do you use to split thick pieces of wood?
87000.e: With the sharp blade of the axe you split the wood lengthways. That way it dries and burns better.
87000.m: You split wood with an axe.

87001.q: What does a car need petrol for?
87001.e: The petrol burns in the engine. The energy released moves the car.

87002.e: Crude oil is pumped out of the ground. In refineries it is turned into petrol and diesel.
87002.m: Petrol is made from crude oil.

87003.q: Where do you fill up with petrol?
87003.e: At the petrol station you fill the car's tank with petrol using a hose.
87003.m: You fill up with petrol at the petrol station.

87004.e: Petrol catches fire from even a small spark. That is why smoking is banned at petrol stations.

87005.q: What comes out of the exhaust when a car burns petrol?
87005.e: Burning petrol produces exhaust fumes. They pollute the air and contribute to climate change.
87005.m: Exhaust fumes come out of the exhaust pipe.

87006.q: Why will petrol one day run short?
a: Crude oil does not grow back
87006.e: Crude oil formed over millions of years. What has been used up does not come back quickly.

87007.q: What does an electric car fill up with instead of petrol?
87007.e: Instead of a tank, an electric car has a large store for electricity. You charge it at a charging station.
87007.m: An electric car runs on electricity.

87008.q: In which unit do you buy petrol?
87008.e: At the pump you can see how many litres you have filled up and how many francs it costs.

87009.q: How does a wind-up car get its energy?
a: You put it in the sun
87009.e: When you turn the key, you put energy into the toy. Then it drives by itself.
87009.m: A wind-up toy gets energy when you turn the key.

87010.q: Which small parts inside a wind-up toy pass the movement on to the wheels?
87010.e: Inside, small cogwheels fit into each other. They pass the movement on to the wheels or legs.
87010.m: Cogwheels pass on the movement in a wind-up toy.

87011.q: What happens when the spring in a wind-up toy unwinds again?
87011.e: The spring slowly gives back its stored energy. This makes the wheels or legs move.
87011.m: The unwinding spring moves the toy.

87012.q: Why does a wind-up toy stop after a while?
a: The spring's energy is used up
87012.e: The spring is then completely unwound again. You have to wind the toy up again.
87012.m: Without a wound-up spring, the toy stops.

87013.q: Where does the energy for winding up actually come from?
87013.e: You turn the key with your hand. The energy from your muscles is then stored in the toy.
87013.m: When winding up, you pass on energy from your muscles.

87014.q: Which thing also works by being wound up?
87014.e: A music box has a spring that you wind up. It turns a cylinder that plays a tune.
87014.m: A music box plays when you wind it up.

87015.q: What can happen if you wind up a wind-up toy far too tightly?
a: It drives backwards into the air
87015.e: A spring can only be tightened up to a certain point. If you force it further, it can break.
87015.m: Wind up a wind-up toy carefully.

87016.q: Does a wind-up toy need batteries?
87016.e: A wind-up toy runs only on the power of its spring. It does not need batteries.
87016.m: A wind-up toy runs without batteries.

87017.q: Why is it good to save energy?
a: It protects the environment and saves money
87017.e: All energy needs raw materials or power stations. Using less protects nature and costs less.
87017.m: Saving energy protects the environment and your wallet.

a: Putting a lid on the pan
87018.e: With a lid, the heat stays in the pan. The water boils faster and uses less electricity.
87018.m: Cooking with a lid saves energy.

87019.q: What uses less energy for hot water?
87019.e: A full bath needs much more hot water than a short shower. Heating water uses a lot of energy.

87020.q: What is the best thing to do with the TV when you have finished?
87020.e: Even on standby, devices use some electricity. Switched off completely, for example with the switch on the power strip, they use none.
87020.m: Switching off completely saves more electricity than standby.

87021.q: How do you save energy with the fridge?
a: Leave the door open for a long time
Put it next to the oven
87021.e: When the door is open, the cold flows out. The fridge then has to work harder and uses more electricity.
87021.m: Close the fridge door again quickly.

87022.q: What is the most energy-saving way to get to school?
87022.e: Walking and cycling use no petrol and no electricity. And the exercise is healthy too.
87022.m: Walking or cycling saves the most energy.

87023.q: What saves heating energy in winter?
a: Not heating the rooms too much
87023.e: Every degree less in the room saves heating energy. A warm jumper helps you feel comfortable anyway.

87024.q: Which letter on the energy label shows an especially economical appliance?
87024.e: The energy label puts appliances into classes A to G. A means very economical, G means high consumption.
87024.m: Energy class A is especially economical.

87025.q: What should you do if you are the last to leave a room?
87025.e: A light in an empty room uses electricity for nothing. One click on the switch saves energy.
87025.m: When you leave the room, switch off the light.

87026.q: Which lamps use the least electricity for the same amount of light?
87026.e: LED lamps turn electricity into lots of light and little heat. That is why they need much less energy than light bulbs.

87027.q: Why do old light bulbs get so hot?
a: They make lots of heat instead of light
87027.e: A light bulb turns electricity mainly into heat. Only a small part becomes light.
87027.m: Light bulbs make more heat than light.

87028.q: What is the best thing to use during the day instead of a lamp?
87028.e: During the day, lots of light comes in through the windows. It costs nothing and uses no electricity.

87029.q: What does a motion sensor do with a light?
a: It switches it on when someone moves
87029.e: The motion sensor notices when someone comes past. After a while without movement it switches the light off again.
87029.m: A motion sensor only switches the light on when needed.

87030.q: Which lamps have mostly not been allowed to be sold in Switzerland for some years?
87030.e: Classic light bulbs waste a lot of energy. That is why they were banned step by step in Switzerland, as in the EU.
87030.m: Classic light bulbs are banned almost everywhere.

87031.q: Is it worth switching off an LED light even for a short time?
87031.e: LED lamps hardly use any extra electricity when switched on. So every minute without light saves energy.
87031.m: Even switching off briefly saves electricity.

87032.q: What is the button on the wall called that you use to switch the light on and off?
87032.e: The light switch cuts off the electricity to the lamp or lets it flow.
87032.m: You switch the light with the light switch.

87033.q: What are most candles made of?
87033.e: Candles are made of wax, for example paraffin, stearin or beeswax. The wax is the candle's fuel.

87034.q: What is the string in the middle of a candle called?
87034.e: The wick draws the liquid wax upwards. There it burns in the flame.
87034.m: The string in a candle is called the wick.

87035.q: What gets less and less on a burning candle?
87035.e: The wax is the fuel. It is slowly used up, which is why the candle gets shorter and shorter.
87035.m: When burning, the wax is used up.

87036.q: Which animals does the wax for some candles come from?
87036.e: Bees build their honeycombs from wax. This beeswax is also used for candles.

87037.q: What happens if you put a glass over a burning candle?
87037.e: A flame needs oxygen from the air. Under the glass it is soon used up, and the flame goes out.
87037.m: Without air, a candle goes out.

87038.q: What must you never do with a burning candle?
a: Put it far away from curtains
87038.e: An unattended candle can start a fire. That is why you put it out before you leave the room.
87038.m: Never leave a burning candle alone.

87039.q: Why does the wax at the top of the candle turn liquid?
a: The heat of the flame melts it
The wax is different at the top
87039.e: The flame gives off heat. This melts the wax directly below it.
87039.m: The heat of the flame melts the wax.

87040.q: In which time before Christmas do you light one more candle each week?
87040.e: Four candles burn on the Advent wreath. Another one is lit on each Sunday in Advent.
87040.m: In Advent you light one more candle each week.

87041.q: Where does a solar lamp in the garden get its energy from?
87041.e: On top of the lamp, a small dark panel catches the sun's light during the day.
87041.m: A solar lamp gets its energy from sunlight.

87042.q: Where does a solar lamp store the energy for the night?
87042.e: During the day the solar cell charges a small battery. At night it supplies the electricity for the light.
87042.m: A solar lamp stores energy in a battery.

87043.q: When does a solar lamp switch on by itself?
87043.e: A small light sensor notices when it gets dark. Then it switches the light on.
87043.m: A solar lamp switches on when it gets dark.

87044.q: Where is the best place to put a solar lamp?
87044.e: The more sun falls on the solar cell, the fuller the battery gets. Then the lamp shines for longer.
87044.m: A solar lamp needs a sunny spot.

87045.q: Why does a solar lamp only shine for a short time after a dull winter's day?
87045.e: In winter the days are short and often grey. The battery then only gets a little charge.
87045.m: Little sun means little light at night.

87046.q: Apart from solar lamps, which small device often runs on a solar cell too?
87046.e: A calculator needs very little electricity. So a small solar cell, which makes electricity even in room light, is often enough.
87046.m: Many calculators run on a solar cell.

87047.q: What helps if the solar cell of a solar lamp is dirty?
87047.e: Dirt and dust block light. A clean solar cell can turn more sunlight into electricity.
87047.m: A clean solar cell makes more electricity.

87048.q: What is the dark panel on top of a solar lamp called?
87048.e: The solar cell is usually dark blue or black. It turns light into electricity.
87048.m: A solar cell sits on top of the solar lamp.

87049.q: What are the four large moons of Jupiter called?
87049.e: The four large moons of Jupiter are called Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto. Titan and Rhea orbit Saturn, Phobos and Deimos orbit Mars, and Triton orbits Neptune.
87049.m: The Galilean moons are called Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto.

87050.q: Under which Galilean moon is there thought to be an ocean where life might be possible?
87050.e: Europa has a smooth crust of ice. Underneath it there is very probably an ocean of salt water, which is why researchers are looking for traces of life there.
87050.m: There is probably an ocean under the ice of Europa.

87051.q: In what order do the Galilean moons orbit Jupiter, from the inside out?
87051.e: Io orbits closest to Jupiter, followed by Europa and Ganymede. Callisto is the furthest away of the four.
87051.m: From the inside out come Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto.

87052.q: Why was the discovery of Jupiter's moons so important for the view of the world at the time?
a: It showed that not everything circles the Earth
It proved that the Moon is made of cheese
It showed that Jupiter is a sun
It proved that the Earth is flat
87052.e: At that time many people believed that all heavenly bodies circled the Earth. But Jupiter's moons could clearly be seen circling another planet, which supported the view with the Sun at the centre.
87052.m: Jupiter's moons showed that there are heavenly bodies that do not circle the Earth.

87053.q: Which simple tool is often enough to see the Galilean moons as points of light next to Jupiter?
87053.e: The four large moons of Jupiter are quite bright. With binoculars held steady, you can make them out as small dots next to Jupiter on clear nights.
87053.m: You can spot the large moons of Jupiter even with binoculars.

87054.q: Which stories do the names Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto come from?
87054.e: The four names stand for figures from Greek mythology who are connected with Zeus, the father of the gods. The Romans called Zeus Jupiter.
87054.m: The Galilean moons have names from Greek mythology.

87055.q: Why are the four large moons of Jupiter called the “Galilean moons”?
a: A ship called Galileo found them
87055.e: Galileo Galilei discovered the four moons with his telescope in 1610. At first he named them after the Medici family, but today they bear his name.
87055.m: The Galilean moons are named after their discoverer Galileo.

87056.q: Which ESA space probe has been on its way since 2023 to explore Jupiter's icy moons?
87056.e: The European probe JUICE took off in April 2023. The University of Bern also worked on one of its instruments.
87056.m: The ESA probe JUICE is exploring the icy moons of Jupiter.

87057.q: How do the orbital periods of Io, Europa and Ganymede relate to each other?
a: Roughly in the ratio 1 to 2 to 4
Roughly in the ratio 1 to 3 to 9
They are all the same length
Roughly in the ratio 1 to 10 to 100
87057.e: While Ganymede circles Jupiter once, Europa manages two laps and Io four. This matching of the orbits is called resonance.
87057.m: Io, Europa and Ganymede orbit in a fixed rhythm of about 1 to 2 to 4.

87058.q: What is there a great deal of on Jupiter's moon Io?
87058.e: Io is the most volcanically active body in the solar system. There are hundreds of volcanoes there and even large lava lakes such as Loki Patera.
87058.m: Io is full of active volcanoes.

87059.q: Where does the heat that drives Io's volcanoes come from?
87059.e: Jupiter and the other moons constantly pull Io in different directions. This kneads and heats the inside of Io, just as a wire that is bent many times gets warm.
87059.m: Io's volcanoes are heated by the kneading effect of tidal forces.

87060.q: Which substance gives Io its yellow to orange colour?
87060.e: Io's volcanoes give off a lot of sulphur and sulphur dioxide. These substances colour the surface yellow, orange, red and white.
87060.m: Sulphur from the volcanoes makes Io yellow and orange.

87061.q: Which space probe was the first to discover active volcanoes on Io, in 1979?
87061.e: In 1979 the engineer Linda Morabito noticed a cloud above the edge of Io in pictures from Voyager 1. It was the plume of an erupting volcano.
87061.m: In 1979 Voyager 1 discovered the first volcanic eruptions beyond the Earth.

87062.q: How high can the plumes from the volcanoes on Io rise?
87062.e: Because Io has only weak gravity and almost no atmosphere, gas and dust are hurled very far out. Some plumes reach heights of up to 500 kilometres.
87062.m: The volcanic plumes on Io rise several hundred kilometres high.

87063.q: How long does Io take for one orbit of Jupiter?
87063.e: Io circles Jupiter in around 1.8 days, which is about 42 hours. That is the fastest orbit of the four Galilean moons.
87063.m: Io races once round Jupiter in less than two days.

87064.q: Unlike the other Galilean moons, what does Io have almost none of?
87064.e: Europa, Ganymede and Callisto contain a lot of water ice. Io, on the other hand, is a very dry rocky moon, because the heat drove the water away long ago.
87064.m: Io is a dry rocky moon with almost no water.

87065.q: How big is Io compared with our Moon?
87065.e: Io is about 3640 kilometres across. The Earth's Moon measures around 3470 kilometres, so Io is only a little bigger.
87065.m: Io is only slightly bigger than our Moon.

87066.q: According to NASA estimates, how much water could the ocean under Europa's ice contain?
a: About twice as much as all the Earth's seas
About as much as Lake Constance
About a hundredth of the Earth's seas
About as much as all the Earth's rivers
87066.e: Europa is smaller than our Moon, but its ocean is probably many dozens of kilometres deep. So it could contain about twice as much water as all the Earth's oceans put together.
87066.m: Europa's ocean probably contains more water than all the Earth's seas.

87067.q: What is the surface of Jupiter's moon Europa made of?
87067.e: Europa is covered by a bright crust of water ice. That is why this moon reflects a lot of sunlight.
87067.m: Europa is covered by a crust of water ice.

87068.q: Why is Europa considered one of the best places to search for alien life?
a: Because there is probably liquid water there
Because it is as warm as the Earth there
Because radio signals have been received from there
87068.e: Liquid water is an important requirement for life as we know it. Simple living things could exist in the ocean under Europa's ice, but that has not been proved.
87068.m: Europa is exciting in the search for life because of its suspected ocean.

87069.q: Which NASA probe took off in October 2024 to study Jupiter's moon Europa more closely?
87069.e: Europa Clipper took off on 14 October 2024. In many close flybys it is to find out whether Europa could be friendly to life.
87069.m: The NASA probe Europa Clipper is on its way to Jupiter's moon Europa.

87070.q: What are the many long lines you can see in pictures of Europa?
87070.e: Europa's ice crust is stretched again and again by Jupiter's tidal forces. It breaks, creating long, often reddish cracks.
87070.m: The lines on Europa are cracks in the ice crust.

87071.q: What do researchers conclude from the fact that Europa has very few impact craters?
a: Europa is never hit by meteorites
The craters are filled with sand
87071.e: Over time, many craters collect on old surfaces. Few craters show that Europa's ice crust is renewed again and again.
87071.m: Few craters show that a surface is young.

87072.q: Which of the four Galilean moons is the smallest?
87072.e: Europa is about 3120 kilometres across. That makes it the smallest of the four and a little smaller than our Moon.
87072.m: Europa is the smallest of the Galilean moons.

87073.q: Which figure from Greek legend, after whom our continent is also named, is the moon Europa named after?
87073.e: In the legend, Zeus in the form of a bull carries the Phoenician princess Europa off to Crete. Her name was later used for the continent and for Jupiter's moon.
87073.m: The moon Europa bears the name of a princess from Greek legend.

87074.q: Which moon is the largest in the whole solar system?
87074.e: Jupiter's moon Ganymede measures around 5270 kilometres. It is just bigger than Saturn's moon Titan and much bigger than our Moon.
87074.m: Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system.

87075.q: Which planet is the moon Ganymede wider than?
87075.e: Ganymede measures about 5270 kilometres, Mercury only about 4880 kilometres. So Ganymede is wider, but has less mass than Mercury.
87075.m: Ganymede is wider than the planet Mercury.

87076.q: What special feature does Ganymede have as the only known moon?
87076.e: In 1996 the Galileo space probe found that Ganymede has its own magnetic field. This has not yet been found on any other known moon.
87076.m: Ganymede is the only known moon with its own magnetic field.

87077.q: Which space probe is to be the first to go into orbit around Ganymede?
87077.e: After circling Jupiter several times, the European probe JUICE is to go into orbit around Ganymede in about 2034. It would be the first time a probe has orbited a moon other than the Earth's Moon.
87077.m: JUICE is to be the first probe to orbit the moon Ganymede.

87078.q: What do researchers think lies deep under Ganymede's ice crust?
a: A huge cave full of air
87078.e: Measurements, including some with the Hubble Telescope, point to a salt water ocean under the surface. It could contain more water than all the Earth's seas.
87078.m: There is probably a salt water ocean under Ganymede's ice.

87079.q: Who was Ganymede in Greek legend?
a: A Trojan prince who became cupbearer to the gods
A giant from the far north
87079.e: According to the legend, Ganymede was a handsome prince from Troy. Zeus brought him to Olympus, where he poured wine for the gods.
87079.m: In the legend, Ganymede was the cupbearer of the gods.

87080.q: How long does Ganymede take for one lap round Jupiter?
87080.e: Ganymede circles Jupiter in about 7.2 days. That is roughly a week.
87080.m: Ganymede circles Jupiter once in about a week.

87081.q: What is Ganymede mainly made of?
87081.e: Ganymede is made of about half rock and half water ice. At its centre it has a core of iron.
87081.m: Ganymede is made of about half rock and half ice.

87082.q: Which of Jupiter's moons is one of the most heavily cratered bodies in the solar system?
87082.e: Callisto's surface is very old and has hardly changed for billions of years. That is why craters lie packed closely together there.
87082.m: Callisto is covered all over with craters.

87083.q: Why is Callisto considered a suitable place for a possible future research station in the Jupiter system?
a: The radiation there is much weaker than at the inner moons
87083.e: Jupiter is surrounded by strong radiation belts. Callisto orbits far out and is geologically quiet, which is why a NASA study in 2003 suggested it as a place for a station.
87083.m: Because of the weak radiation, Callisto is seen as a possible site for a station.

87084.q: Why is Callisto almost geologically inactive?
a: It is far from Jupiter and hardly gets kneaded
87084.e: Far out, Jupiter's tidal forces are only weak. So Callisto hardly gets warmed, and its old surface is preserved.
87084.m: Weak tidal forces make Callisto a quiet moon.

87085.q: How was the huge Valhalla ring basin on Jupiter's moon Callisto formed?
87085.e: A large chunk crashed into Callisto. Many ring-shaped ridges formed around the impact site, and the basin measures over 3000 kilometres.
87085.m: Valhalla on Callisto is a huge impact basin.

87086.q: Which planet is Callisto almost the same size as in diameter?
87086.e: Callisto measures about 4820 kilometres, Mercury about 4880 kilometres. So the two are almost equally wide.
87086.m: Callisto is almost as wide as the planet Mercury.

87087.q: Where does Callisto rank by size among the moons of the solar system?
87087.e: Only Ganymede and Saturn's moon Titan are bigger than Callisto. That puts Callisto in third place.
87087.m: Callisto is the third largest moon in the solar system.

87088.q: Which animal was the nymph Callisto turned into in Greek legend?
87088.e: According to the legend, Callisto was turned into a she-bear. Later she was placed in the sky as the constellation of the Great Bear.
87088.m: In the legend, Callisto became a bear and the constellation of the Great Bear.

87089.q: How long does Callisto take for one orbit of Jupiter?
87089.e: Callisto takes around 16.7 days for one lap round Jupiter. That is the longest orbit of the four Galilean moons.
87089.m: Of the four large moons of Jupiter, Callisto takes longest for one orbit.

87090.q: Roughly how cold is it on the surface of Titan?
87090.e: Titan is almost ten times further from the Sun than the Earth. So it is freezing cold there, at around minus 180 degrees Celsius.
87090.m: It is about minus 180 degrees on Titan.

87091.q: What does Titan have that no other moon in the solar system has?
87091.e: Titan is surrounded by a thick, orange atmosphere. The air pressure at the ground is about one and a half times as high as on Earth.
87091.m: Titan is the only moon with a thick atmosphere.

87092.q: Which gas is Titan's atmosphere mainly made of?
87092.e: Titan's atmosphere is over 90 per cent nitrogen, with some methane. The Earth's air is also mostly nitrogen.

87093.q: What are the lakes on Titan filled with?
87093.e: It is so cold on Titan that methane and ethane are liquid. They form lakes, rivers and even rain there.
87093.m: On Titan there are lakes of liquid methane and ethane.

87094.q: Who discovered Saturn's moon Titan in 1655?
87094.e: The Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens discovered Titan in 1655 with a telescope he had built himself. Titan was the first known moon of Saturn.
87094.m: Christiaan Huygens discovered Saturn's moon Titan in 1655.

87095.q: Which landing probe touched down on Titan in January 2005?
87095.e: The European probe Huygens was carried to Titan by the Cassini space probe. It landed on 14 January 2005 and radioed pictures of the surface.
87095.m: The Huygens probe landed on Saturn's moon Titan in 2005.

87096.q: What is special about NASA's planned Dragonfly mission to Titan?
a: It will drill to the core
87096.e: Dragonfly is a kind of large drone with rotors that is to fly from place to place in Titan's thick air. The launch is planned for 2028.
87096.m: Dragonfly is to fly over Saturn's moon Titan like a drone.

87097.q: Where on Titan are most of the large lakes and seas?
87097.e: The large methane lakes are mainly near Titan's north pole. The largest sea, Kraken Mare, is about as big as the Caspian Sea.
87097.m: Titan's large seas are near the poles.

87098.q: Why could the surface of Titan not be seen before the Cassini mission?
a: A thick orange haze hides it
Titan is too small for telescopes
Titan is always in Saturn's shadow
87098.e: Titan's atmosphere contains a thick haze of organic substances. Only with the radar and special cameras of the Cassini probe could people see through this veil.
87098.m: Thick haze hides the surface of Titan.

87099.q: Which planet does the moon Enceladus orbit?
87099.e: Enceladus is a small, icy moon of Saturn. It is famous for its fountains of water.
87099.m: Enceladus is a moon of Saturn.

87100.q: What are the long cracks at the south pole of Enceladus called?
87100.e: In pictures, the four parallel cracks look like a tiger's stripes. The fountains of water come out of them.
87100.m: The cracks at the south pole of Enceladus are called tiger stripes.

87101.q: What shoots out of cracks into space at the south pole of Saturn's moon Enceladus?
a: Fountains of water vapour and ice
87101.e: Fountains of water vapour and grains of ice come out of the cracks at the south pole. Some of it forms a fine ring around Saturn.
87101.m: Enceladus sprays fountains of water into space.

87102.q: Why does Enceladus shine so brightly?
a: Its fresh icy surface reflects almost all light
It has its own lamps made of gas
It is very hot and glows
It is closer to the Sun than Mercury
87102.e: Enceladus is covered with clean, fresh ice. It reflects almost all the sunlight and is one of the brightest bodies in the solar system.
87102.m: Fresh ice makes Enceladus one of the brightest bodies in space.

87103.e: Enceladus measures around 500 kilometres. That makes it almost seven times narrower than our Moon.
87103.m: Enceladus is a small moon about 500 kilometres across.

87104.q: Roughly how cold is it on the surface of Enceladus?
87104.e: Enceladus is very far from the Sun and gets hardly any warmth. So its icy surface is freezing cold.
87104.m: It is around minus 200 degrees on Enceladus.

87105.q: Which substance important for living things was detected in the ice grains from Enceladus in 2023?
87105.e: Phosphates were found in the ice grains from Enceladus in measurements from the Cassini probe. Phosphorus is a building block of genetic material and cells.
87105.m: Phosphorus, an important building block of life, was found at Enceladus.

87106.q: According to current knowledge, what lies under the ice crust of Enceladus?
a: A global ocean of salt water
A hollow space full of air
87106.e: The slight wobble of Enceladus as it orbits shows that its ice crust is not firmly attached to the core. In between lies an ocean that stretches round the whole moon.
87106.m: Under the ice crust of Enceladus lies an ocean surrounding the whole moon.

87107.q: Where does Phobos rise if you watch from the surface of Mars?
87107.e: Phobos circles Mars faster than the planet spins. That is why it moves backwards across the Martian sky, rising in the west and setting in the east.
87107.m: The Martian moon Phobos rises in the west.

87108.q: What do the Greek names Phobos and Deimos mean?
87108.e: In Greek legend, Phobos and Deimos are sons of the war god Ares, whom the Romans called Mars. Their names mean fear and terror.
87108.m: The moons of Mars are named after Fear and Terror, the companions of the war god.

87109.q: Which planet do the moons Phobos and Deimos orbit?
87109.e: Phobos and Deimos are the two small moons of Mars. They were discovered in 1877.
87109.m: Phobos and Deimos are the moons of Mars.

87110.q: What shape are Phobos and Deimos?
87110.e: The two moons of Mars are too small for their own gravity to pull them into balls. So they look more like lumpy potatoes.
87110.m: Phobos and Deimos are irregularly shaped chunks.

87111.q: Which of the two moons of Mars is the bigger one?
a: Both are exactly the same size
Neither, they are a double moon
87111.e: Phobos measures just over 22 kilometres on average, Deimos only about 12 kilometres. So Phobos is almost twice as big.
87111.m: Phobos is the bigger of the two moons of Mars.

87112.q: How long does Phobos take for one orbit of Mars?
87112.e: Phobos circles Mars in about 7 hours and 39 minutes. That is faster than Mars takes to spin once on its axis.
87112.m: Phobos orbits Mars in less than eight hours.

87113.q: What will probably happen to Phobos in many millions of years?
a: It will crash or break up into a ring
It will fly off into space
It will grow into a large moon
87113.e: Phobos gets a little closer to Mars every year. In a few tens of millions of years it will probably break up or crash onto Mars.
87113.m: Phobos is getting closer to Mars and will one day break up or crash.

87114.q: What is especially striking on the Martian moon Phobos?
87114.e: There is a crater about 9 km across on Phobos. For the small moon that is huge, and the impact almost broke it apart.
87114.m: Phobos has a huge impact crater.

87115.e: Triton is about 2700 kilometres across. It contains well over 99 per cent of the mass of all Neptune's moons.

87116.q: What is unusual about Triton's orbit?
a: It orbits against the direction of Neptune's spin
87116.e: Triton circles Neptune in a retrograde orbit, that is, against the direction in which the planet spins. It is the only large moon in the solar system that does this.
87116.m: Triton is the only large moon with a retrograde orbit.

87117.q: What do researchers conclude about Triton's origin from its retrograde orbit?
a: It was hurled out of Neptune
87117.e: A moon that forms together with its planet normally orbits in the same direction. So Triton was probably a body from the Kuiper Belt that Neptune captured.
87117.m: Triton was probably once a Kuiper Belt object that Neptune captured.

87118.q: Which space probe flew past Triton in 1989?
87118.e: Voyager 2 is still the only probe that has visited Neptune and Triton. It took the first close-up pictures in August 1989.
87118.m: In 1989 Voyager 2 became the only probe to visit Neptune's moon Triton.

87119.q: What did Voyager 2 see on the surface of Triton?
87119.e: On Triton, dark plumes of nitrogen gas and dust shoot up to about 8 kilometres high. These are called geysers or cryovolcanoes.
87119.m: There are nitrogen geysers on Triton.

87120.q: How soon after the discovery of Neptune was Triton found in 1846?
87120.e: Neptune was discovered on 23 September 1846. By 10 October 1846 the Englishman William Lassell had found the moon Triton.
87120.m: Triton was discovered only 17 days after Neptune.

87121.q: Roughly how cold is it on the surface of Triton?
87121.e: Voyager 2 measured about 38 kelvin on Triton, which is around 235 degrees Celsius below zero. That makes Triton one of the coldest places ever measured in the solar system.
87121.m: At about minus 235 degrees, Triton is one of the coldest places in the solar system.

87122.q: Which fruit is part of Triton's surface compared with because of its pattern?
87122.e: A large area of Triton is covered with hollows and ridges. It is like the skin of a cantaloupe melon and is therefore called cantaloupe terrain.
87122.m: Triton has a landscape that looks like melon skin.

87123.q: What will probably happen to Triton in the distant future?
a: Neptune will tear it apart with tidal forces
It will become a planet of its own
It will crash into the Sun
87123.e: Because of its retrograde orbit, Triton is slowly losing height. In a few billion years it will probably come so close that Neptune's tidal forces tear it apart, perhaps forming a ring.
87123.m: Triton is getting closer to Neptune and will one day be torn apart.

87124.q: What is special about the way Pluto and Charon spin?
a: Both always show each other the same side
Neither of them spins at all
Pluto spins faster than the Earth
87124.e: With Pluto and Charon, not only the moon but also the main body is locked. So from one side of Pluto you can always see Charon, and from the other side never.
87124.m: Pluto and Charon always show each other the same side.

87125.q: How big is Charon compared with Pluto?
a: About a tenth of the size
87125.e: Charon measures about 1210 kilometres, Pluto about 2380 kilometres. No other moon is so big compared with its main body.
87125.m: Charon is about half the size of Pluto.

87126.q: Why are Pluto and Charon often called a double system?
a: Their shared centre of gravity lies outside Pluto
87126.e: Because Charon is so big, both circle a point in the open space between them. Pluto itself visibly wobbles around this point.
87126.m: Pluto and Charon circle a shared point between them.

87127.q: Why was Charon discovered so late?
a: It is very far away and very close to Pluto
It only shines during the day
87127.e: From the Earth, Charon can hardly be told apart from Pluto. Only in 1978 did someone notice a small bump on Pluto in photos, and that was the moon.
87127.m: Charon is so close to Pluto that it was overlooked for a long time.

87128.q: Which space probe sent back the first close-up pictures of Charon in July 2015?
87128.e: The NASA probe New Horizons flew past Pluto and Charon on 14 July 2015. It had been travelling for around nine and a half years.
87128.m: In 2015 New Horizons showed Charon close up for the first time.

87129.q: Who is Charon in Greek legend?
87129.e: In the legend, Charon carries the souls of the dead across the River Styx into the underworld. Pluto is the Roman name for the ruler of the underworld, so the name fits well.
87129.m: In the legend, Charon is the ferryman who takes the dead to Pluto's underworld.

87130.q: Where does the reddish colour at Charon's north pole probably come from?
a: From gas drifting over from Pluto
87130.e: Pluto is constantly losing some methane gas, part of which reaches Charon and freezes at the cold pole. Sunlight turns it into reddish-brown substances there.
87130.m: Charon's red pole comes from gas that originates from Pluto.

87131.q: How long does Charon take for one orbit of Pluto?
87131.e: Charon circles Pluto in around 6.4 days. A day on Pluto lasts exactly as long.
87131.m: Charon takes just over six days for one orbit of Pluto.

87132.q: What does “synchronous rotation” mean for the Moon?
a: It always shows the Earth the same side
It does not spin at all
It is firmly attached to the Earth
87132.e: The Moon takes exactly as long to spin once on its axis as it takes for one lap round the Earth. That is why we always see its near side.
87132.m: With synchronous rotation, a moon always shows its planet the same side.

87133.q: Which force slowed down the Moon's spin until it became locked?
87133.e: The Earth's gravity slightly deforms the Moon and pulls on this bulge. Over millions of years this slowed its spin until it matched its orbit.
87133.m: Tidal forces slow a moon's spin until it is locked.

87134.q: Can you see the far side of the Moon from the Earth?
a: No, it stays hidden from the Earth
87134.e: Because of synchronous rotation, the Moon always shows us the same side. Thanks to a slight wobble, you can only see a narrow strip more.
87134.m: You cannot see the far side of the Moon from the Earth.

87135.q: How was the far side of the Moon seen for the first time in 1959?
a: A space probe flew round the Moon and photographed it
With a mirror on a high mountain
87135.e: The Soviet probe Luna 3 flew round the Moon in October 1959. It sent back the first pictures of the side that can never be seen from the Earth.
87135.m: The far side of the Moon was first seen in pictures from a space probe.

87136.q: Why is the expression “dark side of the Moon” actually wrong?
a: The far side is lit by the Sun too
The far side glows by itself
The Moon has no far side at all
The far side is made of bright ice
87136.e: The far side of the Moon is only invisible from the Earth. At new moon it is even fully lit by the Sun.
87136.m: The far side of the Moon is invisible, but not dark.

87137.q: Which country made the first soft landing on the far side of the Moon in 2019?
87137.e: The Chinese probe Chang'e 4 landed on the far side of the Moon in January 2019. It needed its own relay satellite for the radio link to the Earth.
87137.m: In 2019 China became the first country to land on the far side of the Moon.

87138.q: Roughly how long does the Moon take to spin once on its axis?
87138.e: Because of synchronous rotation, the Moon spins once on its axis in around 27.3 days. That is the same as one orbit of the Earth.
87138.m: The Moon spins once on its axis in about 27 days.

87139.q: What long-term effect do the Moon's tides have on the Earth?
a: The days on Earth get longer
The Earth moves closer to the Sun
87139.e: The tides rub against the seabed and very slightly slow the Earth's spin. As a result, a day gets about two thousandths of a second longer every hundred years.
87139.m: The tides slow the Earth, so the days slowly get longer.

87140.q: How do the four Galilean moons spin compared with their orbit of Jupiter?
a: They rotate synchronously like our Moon
They do not spin at all
They spin ten times a day
87140.e: The Galilean moons were also slowed down by Jupiter's strong tidal forces. So each of them always shows Jupiter the same side.
87140.m: Most large moons always show their planet the same side.

87141.q: What did the older capture theory about the origin of the Moon assume?
a: The Earth captured a passing body
The Moon broke away from the Sun
The Moon formed from a volcano
The Moon used to be a comet with a tail
87141.e: According to the capture theory, the Moon formed somewhere else and was then captured by the Earth's gravity. Today this is thought very unlikely, because the Moon and the Earth are too similar in make-up.
87141.m: The capture theory is now thought unlikely.

87142.q: What name did researchers give to the body that collided with the young Earth?
87142.e: The hypothetical body was named after Theia, the mother of the moon goddess Selene in Greek legend. It no longer exists today.
87142.m: The body that collided with the Earth is called Theia.

87143.q: According to the usual idea, roughly how big was Theia?
a: About as big as a mountain
About as big as the Sun
87143.e: The models usually assume a body the size of Mars. That is about half as wide as the Earth.
87143.m: Theia was probably about as big as Mars.

87144.q: Roughly how many years ago did the Earth's Moon form?
87144.e: The Moon formed shortly after the Earth, around 4.5 billion years ago. Dating of Moon rock shows this.
87144.m: The Moon is around 4.5 billion years old.

87145.q: Which observation about Moon rock from the Apollo missions supports the collision theory?
a: Its make-up is very similar to the Earth's mantle
It is made of pure iron
It is much younger than the dinosaurs
87145.e: The rocks from the Moon have almost the same make-up as the Earth's mantle. That fits with the idea that much of the Moon's material was knocked out of the Earth.
87145.m: Moon rock is similar to the Earth's mantle, which supports the collision theory.

87146.q: Why does the Moon have only a small iron core?
a: It formed mainly from light mantle rock
It lost its iron to the Sun
There is no iron in space
87146.e: In the collision, mainly outer rock was hurled into space, while the heavy iron mostly stayed in the Earth. That is why the Moon is low in iron and has a low density.
87146.m: The Moon is low in iron because it formed mainly from mantle rock.

87147.q: What happened to the debris after the great collision, before the Moon formed?
a: It formed a ring around the Earth
It all fell into the Sun
87147.e: The debris that was hurled out gathered in a disc around the Earth. The Moon clumped together from it in a relatively short time.
87147.m: The Moon clumped together from a ring of debris around the Earth.

87148.q: What did the old fission theory about the formation of the Moon assume?
a: The Moon broke away from the fast-spinning Earth
The Moon fell down from the Sun
The Moon formed from a comet
The Moon was hurled out of Jupiter
87148.e: In the 19th century people thought that the young Earth spun so fast that a piece broke off. Today this idea is considered disproved.
87148.m: The fission theory of the Moon's formation is now considered disproved.

87149.q: What do igneous rocks form from?
87149.e: Igneous rocks form when magma inside the Earth or lava at the surface cools and becomes solid. They are also called solidified rocks.
87149.m: Igneous rocks form when molten rock solidifies.

87150.q: What are igneous rocks that have solidified slowly deep in the Earth’s crust called?
87150.e: Plutonic rocks, also called intrusive rocks, cool very slowly deep below the surface. A well-known example is granite.
87150.m: Plutonic rocks solidify slowly deep in the Earth’s crust.

87151.q: What are igneous rocks that have solidified from lava at the Earth’s surface called?
87151.e: Extrusive rocks, also called volcanic rocks, form from lava that flows out during volcanic eruptions. They cool quickly.
87151.m: Extrusive rocks form from lava at the Earth’s surface.

87152.q: Why do plutonic rocks usually have large, clearly visible crystals?
a: They are polished by the wind
They contain a lot of water
87152.e: When molten rock cools slowly, the crystals have a lot of time to grow. That is why you can see the individual grains in granite clearly.
87152.m: Slow cooling lets large crystals grow.

87153.q: What is the black, glassy rock that forms when lava cools extremely quickly called?
87153.e: With very fast cooling, no crystals can form, and volcanic glass is created. Obsidian has sharp broken edges and was used for blades in the Stone Age.

87154.q: Which volcanic rock is so full of gas bubbles that it can float on water?
87154.e: Pumice forms from gas-rich lava that froths up during an eruption. The many holes make it so light that it floats.
87154.m: Pumice is so porous that it can float.

87155.q: Which mountain range is the volcanic rock andesite named after?
87155.e: Andesite is a grey extrusive rock that is very common in the volcanoes of the Andes in South America. That is where it gets its name.
87155.m: Andesite is named after the Andes in South America.

87156.q: Which dark extrusive rock makes up a large part of the seabed and volcanic islands such as Hawaii?
87156.e: Basalt forms from runny lava that solidifies quickly. It is dark, fine-grained and the most common volcanic rock on Earth.
87156.m: Basalt is a dark rock made of solidified lava.

a: From rock that is changed by heat
From metal that melts in the Earth’s core
87157.e: Sand, mud, gravel or shells are deposited in layers. Under the weight of new layers, they are pressed together and cemented.
87157.m: Sedimentary rocks form from deposited, hardened particles.

87158.q: What forms when loose sand is pressed together and cemented over a long time?
87158.e: New layers press down with their weight on the sand below. Water is squeezed out, and minerals cement the grains together. Over time, sand becomes sandstone.
87158.m: Pressed and cemented sand becomes sandstone.

87159.q: What can you often see clearly in sedimentary rocks in a rock face?
a: Layers lying on top of each other
87159.e: Sediments are deposited layer by layer. That is why sedimentary rocks often show clear layers, as you can see in the Jura, for example.
87159.m: Sedimentary rocks are often built up in clear layers.

87160.q: What is Nagelfluh, which you can see on the Rigi or in Toggenburg, for example?
a: A rock made of cemented pebbles
A rock made of solidified lava
A rock made of glacier ice
A rock made of pure salt
87160.e: Millions of years ago, rivers deposited lots of round pebbles. These were cemented together with sand and lime. The stones look like nail heads in a wall.
87160.m: Nagelfluh is made of cemented pebbles.

87161.e: When the water in a cut-off sea basin evaporates, the dissolved salt is left behind. Such salt deposits are found near Bex in Vaud, for example.
87161.m: Rock salt is left behind when seawater evaporates.

87162.q: Which sedimentary rock is made of the very finest particles?
87162.e: Clay particles are tiny and only settle in very still water. Once hardened, they form claystone.
87162.m: Claystone is made of the finest clay particles.

87163.q: What material did coal mainly form from?
87163.e: Millions of years ago, huge amounts of dead plants piled up in swamps. Without air, under pressure and heat, they turned into peat and then coal.
87163.m: Coal is a sedimentary rock made of ancient plant remains.

87164.q: Which sedimentary rock makes up a large part of the Jura mountains?
87164.e: In the Jura, lime mud and shells were deposited in a warm sea. This became limestone, which was later folded up into mountains.
87164.m: The Jura is mostly made of limestone.

87165.q: Roughly what share of the Earth’s land surface is covered by sedimentary rocks?
87165.e: Sedimentary rocks form only a thin skin on the Earth’s crust. But this skin covers about three quarters of the land surface.
87165.m: Sedimentary rocks cover about three quarters of the land.

a: By being changed under high pressure and high temperature
By being deposited in a lake
87166.e: When a rock gets deep into the Earth, pressure and heat change its minerals and structure. But it does not melt completely.
87166.m: Metamorphic rocks form by being changed under pressure and heat.

87167.q: What does the Greek word metamorphosis mean?
87167.e: Metamorphosis means transformation or change of form. The word is also used for a caterpillar changing into a butterfly.

87168.q: Which metamorphic rock forms from sandstone?
87168.e: Sandstone is made mainly of grains of quartz. Under pressure and heat, they grow together into a very hard rock, quartzite.

87169.q: What happens if a rock deep down is not just changed but melts completely?
87169.e: Metamorphism only takes place in the solid state. If the rock melts completely, magma forms, which later becomes an igneous rock.
87169.m: If a rock melts completely, it becomes magma.

87170.q: Where do metamorphic rocks form in large amounts?
a: Deep inside mountains as they are built
At the bottom of shallow lakes
87170.e: When continental plates collide, rocks are pushed deep down and strongly squeezed. This regional metamorphism also shaped many rocks of the Alps.
87170.m: Large amounts of metamorphic rock form when mountains are built.

87171.q: What is the change of rock that lies right next to hot magma called?
87171.e: When magma pushes into the Earth’s crust, the rock next to it is strongly heated. Where it touches the molten rock, it is changed.
87171.m: Contact metamorphism is caused by the heat of nearby magma.

87172.q: Why are the minerals in many metamorphic rocks lined up in parallel?
a: Because of pressure from one particular direction
Because of gravity as they fall
Because of wind at the surface
Because of the current in rivers
87172.e: When a rock is strongly squeezed from one side, flat minerals line up across the pressure. This makes the rock look striped or layered.
87172.m: Pressure from one direction lines up the minerals in metamorphic rocks.

87173.q: Why did people in Ticino and the Grisons build stoves from the soft stone called lavez?
87173.e: Lavez, also called soapstone or pot stone, is soft and stores heat very well. Cooking pots used to be turned from it, and stoves are still built from it today.
87173.m: Lavez is a soft stone that stores heat well.

87174.q: Which of the following groups of rocks can be changed by metamorphism?
87174.e: Igneous, sedimentary and even metamorphic rocks can be changed again. What matters is that pressure and temperature change a lot.
87174.m: Any kind of rock can be changed by metamorphism.

87175.q: What does the rock cycle describe?
a: How rocks change into one another over a long time
How stones roll in a stream
How crystals grow in a laboratory
87175.e: Rocks are worn away, deposited, buried, changed, melted and lifted again. So the same material becomes new rocks again and again.
87175.m: In the rock cycle, rocks change again and again.

87176.q: What are the three main groups of rocks in the rock cycle?
87176.e: Rocks are grouped by how they formed. Solidified molten rock, hardened deposits and changed rocks make up the three groups.
87176.m: There are igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks.

87177.q: Which rock forms when sand is deposited on the seabed and hardens over a long time?
87177.e: Layer by layer, the sand is pressed together and cemented. This forms a sedimentary rock, sandstone.

87178.q: Which two sources of energy drive the rock cycle?
a: The heat inside the Earth and energy from the Sun
87178.e: The Earth’s heat melts and moves rock deep down. The Sun drives the weather and the water cycle, and with them weathering and erosion at the surface.
87178.m: The Earth’s heat and the Sun’s energy keep the rock cycle going.

87179.q: Roughly how long does it take for a rock to go once through the cycle?
87179.e: Erosion, deposition, burial and uplift happen extremely slowly. A full round usually takes many millions to hundreds of millions of years.
87179.m: One round of the rock cycle takes millions of years.

87180.q: Where is rock from the Earth’s crust pushed back into the mantle in large amounts?
a: At the bottom of mountain lakes
87180.e: At subduction zones, one tectonic plate sinks beneath another. Rock goes down to great depths, where it is changed or melted.
87180.m: At subduction zones, rock sinks into the Earth’s mantle.

87181.q: How do rocks that were changed deep in the Earth get back to the surface?
a: Through uplift and erosion of the layers above
87181.e: When mountains are built, blocks of rock are lifted up. At the same time, water and ice wear away the upper layers until the deep rocks become visible.
87181.m: Uplift and erosion bring deep rocks to the surface.

87182.q: In the rock cycle, what happens to a sedimentary rock that is buried deep and strongly heated?
87182.e: With increasing depth, pressure and temperature rise. The sedimentary rock is changed; for example, limestone becomes marble.
87182.m: Buried sedimentary rocks become metamorphic rocks.

87183.q: What happens to a rock at the Earth’s surface that is exposed to wind, water and frost?
a: It is slowly broken up and worn away
87183.e: At the surface, weather and water attack every rock. The fragments are carried away and later deposited as sediment.
87183.m: At the surface, every rock is slowly broken up and worn away.

87184.e: Basalt contains many dark minerals that are rich in iron and magnesium. That is why it is dark grey to black.
87184.m: Basalt is a dark, almost black rock.

87185.q: What is the floor of the oceans mostly made of?
87185.e: At the mid-ocean ridges, basalt lava constantly comes out. It forms the oceanic crust, which makes up most of the seabed.
87185.m: The seabed is mostly made of basalt.

87186.q: What shape do thick basalt flows often take as they cool slowly?
87186.e: As it cools, the lava shrinks and cracks. The cracks often form a pattern of mostly six-sided columns.
87186.m: Cooling basalt often breaks into six-sided columns.

87187.q: Where is the famous Giant’s Causeway with about 40,000 basalt columns?
87187.e: The Giant’s Causeway lies on the north coast of Northern Ireland. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
87187.m: The Giant’s Causeway in Northern Ireland is made of basalt columns.

87188.q: Which island in the North Atlantic is made mostly of basalt?
87188.e: Iceland lies on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and on a hotspot. The many volcanic eruptions built the island out of basalt lava.
87188.m: Iceland is an island made of basalt.

87189.q: How does the lava of basalt volcanoes such as those on Hawaii usually behave?
a: It is runny and flows in long streams
It stays as a solid plug in the crater
It only flies into the air as ash
It is cold and does not flow at all
87189.e: Basalt lava is very hot and contains few substances that make it thick. So it flows easily and forms long lava flows.

87190.q: What are the dark areas on the Moon called lunar seas really?
87190.e: More than three billion years ago, runny lava filled huge impact basins on the Moon. The dark basalt stands out clearly from the lighter highlands.
87190.m: The lunar seas are plains of dark basalt.

87191.q: Which insulation material for houses is made from melted basalt and similar rock?
87191.e: Basalt is melted at a very high temperature and blown into fine fibres. This makes rock wool, which protects houses from cold and fire.
87191.m: Basalt can be used to make rock wool for insulation.

87192.q: How can you usually recognise gneiss?
a: By its light and dark stripes
87192.e: In gneiss, light minerals such as quartz and feldspar and dark ones such as mica are arranged in layers. This gives it a striped look.
87192.m: You can recognise gneiss by its light and dark stripes.

87193.q: What does granite become when it is strongly squeezed and heated deep in the Earth?
87193.e: Under high pressure and high temperature, the minerals of granite line up in layers. This turns it into gneiss.

87194.q: Where did the gneiss in the upper part of the Matterhorn originally come from?
87194.e: The summit pyramid of the Matterhorn is made of gneiss from the Dent Blanche nappe. This rock was once part of a piece of Africa that was pushed over European rock when the Alps formed.
87194.m: The gneiss at the top of the Matterhorn originally came from the African Plate.

87195.q: What is so-called “Ticino granite” usually, from a geological point of view?
87195.e: The building stones quarried in Ticino are often sold as granite. But geologically they are gneisses, taken from the quarries in Ticino’s valleys.

87196.q: What are the traditional roofs of many stone houses in Ticino covered with?
87196.e: Gneiss can be split along its layers into thick slabs. These heavy stone slabs cover the roofs of many rustici in Ticino.
87196.m: Many rustici in Ticino have roofs made of gneiss slabs.

87197.q: Which rocks does the Acasta gneiss in Canada belong to?
a: The oldest known rocks on Earth
87197.e: The Acasta gneiss in north-western Canada is about 4 billion years old. That makes it one of the oldest known rocks on Earth.
87197.m: The Acasta gneiss is one of the oldest rocks on Earth.

87198.q: What are the “eyes” in augen gneiss?
a: Drops of water in the stone
87198.e: In some gneisses, single feldspar crystals have been shaped into oval lenses. The stripes flow around them, so they look like eyes.
87198.m: The eyes in augen gneiss are oval feldspar crystals.

87199.q: Does gneiss form at a lower or higher temperature than slate?
87199.e: Slate forms through weak metamorphism. Gneiss only forms through strong metamorphism, often at temperatures of several hundred degrees deep in the Earth’s crust.
87199.m: Gneiss forms through strong metamorphism at high temperature.

87200.q: In which part of Switzerland do you find especially a lot of gneiss?
87200.e: In the Central Alps, for example around the Gotthard or in Ticino, deeply buried rocks have come to the surface through uplift. Many of them are gneisses.
87200.m: Gneiss is widespread in the Swiss Central Alps.

87201.q: Which property is typical of slate?
a: It can be split into thin slabs
87201.e: The minerals in slate are lined up in parallel. Along these surfaces the rock can be split into thin, smooth slabs.
87201.m: Slate can be split into thin slabs.

87202.q: Which rock does slate form from?
87202.e: When claystone is squeezed deep down and slightly heated, slate forms. It is one of the weakly changed rocks.

87203.q: What did schoolchildren often write on in the past, before exercise books became cheap?
87203.e: Slates were smooth, dark and could be wiped clean again and again. Many came from slate mines, including some in Switzerland.
87203.m: Schoolchildren used to write on slates.

87204.q: What did people use to write on a slate in the past?
87204.e: The slate pencil was a thin stick, often made of soft slate itself. It left pale lines on the slate.
87204.m: You wrote on a slate with a slate pencil.

87205.q: What was slate from the Glarus region mainly used for in the past?
a: For writing slates, tables and roofs
87205.e: At the Landesplattenberg near Engi, slate was mined for centuries for writing slates, tables and roofs. Today you can visit the mine.
87205.m: Slate was mined in the Glarus region for a long time.

87206.q: Which fossils are especially well known in Glarus slate?
87206.e: Glarus slate formed from fine mud in a sea. Fish were preserved especially well in it.
87206.m: Fossil fish are found in Glarus slate.

87207.q: Bündner schist shapes many mountains in the Grisons. What did it originally form from?
a: From the deposits of an ancient sea
From the lava of a volcano
From the sand dunes of a desert
87207.e: Bündner schist formed from the deposits of an ancient sea and was changed when the Alps were formed. It makes up large parts of the mountains of the Grisons.
87207.m: Bündner schist formed from the deposits of an ancient sea.

87208.q: Why does mica schist glitter in the light?
a: It contains lots of tiny mica flakes
87208.e: Mica schist has been changed more strongly than slate. The mica flakes that grew in it reflect the light and make it glitter.
87208.m: Mica schist glitters because of its mica flakes.

87209.q: Which type of rock does Nagelfluh belong to?
87209.e: A conglomerate is made of rounded stones cemented together by a binding material. Nagelfluh is such a sedimentary rock.
87209.m: Nagelfluh is a conglomerate made of rounded stones.

87210.q: Where does Nagelfluh get its name from?
a: The stones look like nail heads in a rock face
It was used for making nails
It is as hard as iron nails
It was discovered by a Mr Nagel
87210.e: When the pebbles stick out of the rock face, they look like the heads of nails. In German, Nagel means nail, and Fluh is a Swiss word for rock.
87210.m: Nagelfluh means rock with stones like nail heads.

87211.q: Why are the stones in Nagelfluh round?
a: They were carried a long way by rivers
They are made of drops of lava
87211.e: While being carried by rivers, the stones knock against each other and lose their edges. So they became round pebbles before they were deposited.
87211.m: The stones in Nagelfluh were ground round in rivers.

87212.q: Where do the pebbles of Swiss Nagelfluh come from?
a: From the Alps, which were forming at the time
From the seabed of the Atlantic
87212.e: While the Alps were being lifted up, rivers carried huge amounts of debris into the land in front of them. There they deposited it in large fans of debris.
87212.m: The pebbles of Nagelfluh come from the young Alps.

87213.q: Which mountain on the border between the cantons of Bern and Lucerne is made of Nagelfluh?
87213.e: The Napf is a large former fan of debris made of Nagelfluh. Its deeply cut ravines are typical of this rock.
87213.m: The Napf is a mountain made of Nagelfluh.

87214.q: In which landslide in the canton of Schwyz did layers of Nagelfluh slide off the Rossberg in 1806?
87214.e: On 2 September 1806, layers of Nagelfluh slid off the Rossberg on softened marl. The landslide destroyed Goldau and killed around 450 people.
87214.m: In the Goldau landslide of 1806, Nagelfluh slid off the Rossberg.

87215.q: Because of its look, what do Swiss people jokingly call Nagelfluh?
87215.e: Nagelfluh looks like concrete with gravel in it. That is why it is jokingly called the Lord’s concrete, meaning concrete made by nature.
87215.m: Nagelfluh is also called the Lord’s concrete.

87216.q: What holds the pebbles in Nagelfluh together?
a: A natural binding material made of lime and sand
87216.e: Fine sand and lime were deposited between the pebbles. Over time this mass became hard and cemented the stones together.
87216.m: Lime and sand cement the stones of Nagelfluh together.

87217.q: What does molasse mean in geology?
a: Debris worn away from the Alps, lying in front of them
Glacier ice in the Central Plateau
87217.e: As the Alps were lifted up, a lot of rock was worn away. This debris filled the basin north of the Alps and became rock: the molasse.
87217.m: The molasse is made of debris worn away from the Alps.

87218.q: In which large region of Switzerland does the molasse form the ground underneath?
87218.e: The Central Plateau lies in the molasse basin between the Alps and the Jura. Under the Ice Age deposits there is molasse almost everywhere.
87218.m: The Swiss Central Plateau lies on molasse.

87219.q: Which rocks are mainly found in the molasse?
87219.e: Depending on the current, rivers deposited coarse pebbles, sand or fine mud. These became Nagelfluh, sandstone and marl.
87219.m: Sandstone, marl and Nagelfluh are found in the molasse.

87220.q: Which rock are many houses in Bern’s old town built from?
87220.e: After the great fire of 1405, Bern was rebuilt with sandstone from the surrounding area. This Bern sandstone formed from Alpine debris in a shallow sea.
87220.m: Bern’s old town is built from molasse sandstone.

87221.q: Roughly when was the molasse deposited?
87221.e: The molasse formed while the Alps were being folded up. Deposition began about 34 million years ago and ended about 5 million years ago.
87221.m: The molasse formed about 35 to 5 million years ago.

87222.q: What covered the area of today’s Central Plateau for a while about 20 million years ago?
87222.e: About 20 million years ago, the sea flowed into the basin north of the Alps. That is why shells and even sharks’ teeth are found in these layers.
87222.m: About 20 million years ago, there was a sea in the Central Plateau.

87223.q: Which mountain on the edge of the Alps is made of tilted layers of molasse?
87223.e: On the northern edge of the Alps, the molasse layers were pushed together and tilted when the mountains formed. The Rigi is made of such layers of Nagelfluh.
87223.m: The Rigi is made of tilted molasse.

87224.q: How far does the molasse basin north of the Alps stretch?
a: Only from Lake Constance to Zurich
87224.e: The molasse basin runs as a long trough, about 1000 kilometres long, along the northern edge of the Alps. It begins in the west at Lake Geneva and reaches through southern Germany to Austria.
87224.m: The molasse basin stretches from Lake Geneva to Austria.

a: Rock breaking down where it is
87225.e: In weathering, rock is loosened and broken down by weather, water and living things. At first it stays in the same place.
87225.m: Weathering is rock breaking down where it is.

87226.q: What is the difference between weathering and erosion?
a: Weathering breaks rock up, erosion carries it away
Weathering only happens in the sea
87226.e: Weathering prepares the rock by loosening it. Only in erosion do water, ice or wind carry the particles away.
87226.m: Weathering loosens rock, erosion carries it away.

87227.q: What kind of weathering is it when rainwater slowly dissolves limestone?
87227.e: Rainwater contains a little carbonic acid, which can dissolve lime. Because the substances change in the process, it is called chemical weathering.
87227.m: Rainwater dissolving lime is chemical weathering.

87228.q: What is it called when plant roots push rocks apart?
87228.e: Roots grow into fine cracks and get thicker. With great force they widen the cracks until the rock breaks. This is a type of biological weathering.
87228.m: In root wedging, plant roots break rock apart.

87229.q: Why do rocks in deserts often break apart through temperature weathering?
a: Because of big differences between day and night
87229.e: In deserts, rock gets very hot during the day and cools down a lot at night. Constant expanding and shrinking causes cracks.
87229.m: Strong temperature changes make rock break apart in deserts.

87230.q: In salt weathering, what breaks the rock apart?
a: Salt crystals growing in the pores
87230.e: Salty water gets into the pores and evaporates. The growing salt crystals push the rock apart, especially on coasts and in dry areas.
87230.m: Growing salt crystals can break rock apart.

87231.q: In which climate is chemical weathering strongest?
a: In the hot, humid climate of the tropics
In the cold climate of the polar regions
In the dry climate of deserts
In high mountains above the snow line
87231.e: Chemical processes happen faster in warmth and need water. That is why rock breaks down especially deeply in the hot, humid tropics.
87231.m: Chemical weathering is strongest in the tropics.

87232.q: Over a long time, what does rainwater carve out of bare limestone rocks such as those on the Schrattenfluh?
87232.e: Rainwater contains a little carbonic acid and slowly dissolves the lime. This creates grooves that can be up to a metre deep. They are called karren.
87232.m: Rainwater carves grooves into limestone rocks.

87233.e: When water, wind or ice can no longer carry material, it settles. This process is called sedimentation.
87233.m: Sedimentation is the depositing of particles.

87234.q: When does a river deposit especially a lot of material?
87234.e: Fast water can carry a lot of material. When the current slows down, for example where it flows into a lake, the particles sink to the bottom.

87235.q: Which particles settle first in a river that is slowing down?
a: All of them at the same time
87235.e: Large stones and gravel sink first, because the water can only carry them with a lot of force. Fine sand and clay are carried further.
87235.m: Coarse particles settle first, fine ones later.

87236.q: What is the landform called that forms when a river deposits a lot of material at its mouth?
87236.e: At its mouth, the river loses its force and deposits material. Land grows out into the lake or sea, like the Maggia delta near Locarno.
87236.m: A delta forms from deposits at a river mouth.

87237.q: Why is a large delta growing where the Kander flows into Lake Thun?
a: The Kander deposits a lot of gravel and sand there
A glacier pushes debris into the lake there
The wind blows sand in there
87237.e: Since 1714, the Kander has flowed into Lake Thun through a man-made cut. In the calm lake water it deposits so much material that a large delta has formed.
87237.m: Since 1714, the Kander has been building a delta into Lake Thun.
